descriptors.title: Define problems with user stories
descriptors.description: Define problems with given or co-developed design criteria and by creating user stories
descriptors.knowledge: Students can define problems with given design criteria and by co-creating user stories (AC9TDI4P01). They have worked with provided design criteria and contributed to user stories collaboratively. They have not yet developed design criteria with more agency (co-developed rather than given) or created user stories independently from stimulus.
descriptors.endpoint: Students define a problem by co-developing or applying design criteria and by creating user stories that identify an issue, the user, and their need.

nodes.label: Identifying a problem from stimulus
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify an issue from a stimulus and frame it as a problem that a digital solution could address
criteria: Identifies a specific issue from the stimulus
States the problem in terms of a user need, not just a system gap
nodes.hinge_reason: Problem framing in N1 cascades into N2 (user story) and N3 (design criteria) — a student who frames the problem incorrectly will write user stories for the wrong user and criteria that cannot evaluate the actual need. All downstream design work inherits the N1 framing.

width.minimum: Given a stimulus (e.g. an article, scenario), identify an issue and state the problem a solution needs to address
width.typical: Use stimulus material to identify an issue, name the affected users, and describe the problem in terms of what users need — not just what is wrong
wider: Investigate how feral animals threaten native flora and fauna and identify the problem from the perspective of different stakeholders — rangers, farmers, ecologists — developing a problem statement that reflects one user group's needs
Examine how a community in a bushfire or flood-prone area needs an emergency preparedness solution — defining the problem from the perspective of the family user rather than the system designer

modes.reason: Students tend to frame problems from a system-designer perspective ('we need an app') rather than a user perspective ('the family needs to know what to do'). Stimulus materials with emotionally real, socially meaningful contexts — emergencies, environmental threats — help students stay anchored to the user's actual experience and need.

nodes.label: Writing a user story
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a user story that identifies who the user is, what they need, and why
criteria: Writes a user story that identifies the user, their need, and the reason for the need
The user story is consistent with the identified problem
nodes.hinge_reason: User stories in N2 are the direct input for N3's criteria co-development — criteria are derived from what the user stories identify as needs. Students who produce vague or missing user stories cannot develop meaningful criteria in N3.

width.minimum: Write a user story in standard form: 'As a [user], I need [something] so that [reason]' — linked to an identified problem
width.typical: Write one or more user stories that capture the core needs of the user group; use the user stories to clarify what the solution must do versus what would be nice to have
wider: Write user stories for a roadside bushfire or flood risk rating system from the perspectives of two different user groups (e.g. a traveller vs a local resident) — identifying where their needs diverge
Discuss user stories that reflect different cultural or accessibility needs — e.g. a user who reads in a language other than English or a user with a visual impairment

modes.reason: The user story format is a reasoning scaffold, not just a template. Students who use it mechanically produce technically compliant stories that miss the 'why' — the reason the user needs the feature is what connects the story to the design criteria. Unpacking the three-part structure explicitly (who / what / why) helps students use it as a thinking tool.

nodes.label: Co-developing design criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can contribute to co-developing design criteria that can be used to evaluate solutions
criteria: States at least two design criteria that connect to the identified user stories
Can explain what each criterion means for what the solution must do

width.minimum: Given a problem and user stories, identify at least two design criteria that a solution must satisfy; explain how each criterion connects to the user stories
width.typical: Discuss and co-develop a set of design criteria based on user stories and practical constraints (e.g. cost, sustainability, timeliness); use the criteria to distinguish between requirements and preferences
wider: Discuss design criteria for a bushfire/flood risk rating system — weighing timeliness (must update quickly), reliability (must work offline) and accessibility (must suit low-literacy users) as competing criteria
Consider how design criteria for a digital solution change when the user community has different infrastructure access — e.g. low-bandwidth constraints in remote areas

modes.reason: Design criteria integrate the user stories (what the user needs) with practical constraints (what is feasible). This is the node where problem definition becomes actionable for design — students who cannot connect stories to criteria will generate design ideas disconnected from user needs.

descriptors.title: Design algorithms with branching and iteration
descriptors.description: Design algorithms involving multiple alternatives (branching) and iteration
descriptors.knowledge: Students can follow and describe algorithms involving sequencing, comparison operators (branching) and iteration (AC9TDI4P02). They have worked with existing algorithms and described how they work. They have not yet designed algorithms themselves — the shift from reading/describing to creating is the new demand at this band.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design algorithms that include multiple branches (more than two alternatives) and loops (repetition until a condition is met), representing their logic as structured steps.

nodes.label: Iteration — loops until a condition is met
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design an algorithm that repeats steps until a condition is met
criteria: Specifies what step(s) repeat in the loop
Specifies a clear condition that ends the loop
Identifies what value changes across iterations
nodes.hinge_reason: Loop design in N1 is a prerequisite component for N3's combined branching+iteration algorithm — students who cannot design a correct loop (with stopping condition) cannot produce a valid combined algorithm. The stopping condition error introduced here carries directly into N3.

width.minimum: Design an algorithm that includes a loop with a clear condition for stopping — e.g. keep mixing UNTIL combined, subtract UNTIL result is zero
width.typical: Design algorithms with iteration for a range of problem types — counting loops (repeat N times), condition loops (repeat until X), and nested actions within the loop; represent the loop structure clearly in pseudocode, flowchart, or structured English
wider: Design an algorithm for First Nations rangers to monitor live tracking data for feral animals — repeating a check-and-respond loop until a target is captured or leaves the area
Design an algorithm that uses a loop to process each item in a dataset (e.g. each plant in a survey grid) and accumulates a result across iterations

modes.reason: Students designing loops for the first time often specify the loop action correctly but omit or mis-specify the stopping condition. Explicitly scaffolding the loop design as: (1) what step repeats? (2) what condition must be checked? (3) what value changes each iteration? — prevents loops with no exit condition.

nodes.label: Multiple alternatives — branching beyond yes/no
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design an algorithm with more than two branches (multiple alternatives, not just binary if/else)
criteria: Designs an algorithm with at least three distinct branches
Conditions for branches are mutually exclusive (no two conditions can both be true for the same input)
nodes.hinge_reason: Multi-branch design in N2 is the second prerequisite component for N3 — students who cannot write mutually exclusive multi-branch conditions will produce overlapping branches when combining with iteration in N3, causing algorithms that fire incorrect branches.

width.minimum: Design an algorithm with at least three alternatives — e.g. IF distance < 2km THEN walk, ELSE IF distance < 5km THEN ride, ELSE catch the bus
width.typical: Design multi-branch decision logic for a real problem context, using nested IF/ELSE IF/ELSE structure; trace through the algorithm with at least three different inputs to verify the correct branch fires for each
wider: Design an algorithm for a garden watering decision system that considers multiple inputs — humidity level AND soil moisture level — requiring nested conditions, not just a single threshold
Design an algorithm modelling how rangers decide how to respond when feral animal tracking data shows different threat levels (approaching slowly / approaching quickly / already at site / retreating)

modes.reason: Students who have only written binary (if/else) branches struggle to see how to chain alternatives. Problem contexts with three or more clearly distinct outcomes (transport mode, threat level, grade bands) make the multi-branch structure feel natural rather than arbitrary.

The critical error in multi-branch design is overlapping conditions — students write branches where multiple conditions could be true simultaneously. Tracing through edge cases (exactly 2km, exactly 5km) using a structured verify-step prevents this.

nodes.label: Algorithms with both branching and iteration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design an algorithm that combines branching and iteration, responding to data
criteria: Designs an algorithm that includes at least one loop and one branch
Can trace through the algorithm with a specific input and identify which steps execute

width.minimum: Design an algorithm that contains at least one loop and at least one branch within or around it — e.g. repeat a check loop, and branch based on the check result
width.typical: Design an algorithm that uses iteration to process a series of inputs and branching to respond differently to each input; evaluate whether one algorithm is better than another for the same problem and explain why
wider: Compare two algorithms that solve the same problem — one using nested loops and one using a single loop with multi-branch conditions — and explain which is clearer or more efficient for a given scenario
Design an algorithm that responds to live data (e.g. sensor readings) using a loop that repeats until a condition is met, with branches that determine the response at each iteration

modes.reason: This node integrates the two structural elements — loops and branches — into a single algorithm. Students who have designed each element separately may not know how to nest them. Tracing through a combined algorithm step by step (what happens at this iteration? which branch fires?) is the integration act.

descriptors.title: Design a user interface
descriptors.description: Design a user interface for a digital system
descriptors.knowledge: Students can generate, communicate and compare designs (AC9TDI4P03). They have produced design ideas and communicated them. They have not yet focused specifically on designing user interfaces — the layout, accessibility, and usability considerations of how a user interacts with a digital system.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design a user interface for a digital system that addresses an identified need, considering layout, accessibility, and how users from different backgrounds can access the information.

nodes.label: What a user interface is and does
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that a user interface is the part of a digital system the user interacts with, and identify key elements of a user interface design
criteria: Names at least three user interface elements correctly
Explains the purpose of each identified element
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify UI elements and their purposes cannot produce a purposeful design in N2 — interface design requires knowing what the components are and what they do for the user. Without N1, N2 produces decorative layouts rather than functional designs.

width.minimum: Identify at least three elements of a user interface (e.g. buttons, menus, input fields, labels) in an existing app or system; explain the purpose of each element
width.typical: Analyse an existing user interface (e.g. a school canteen ordering app) and identify how the layout, labels, and controls guide the user toward completing a task; discuss what would make it easier or harder to use
wider: Investigate how consistent symbols (copy, paste, save icons) across different apps help users from different cultural and language backgrounds — exploring what happens when symbols are ambiguous or culturally specific
Examine the user interface of a telehealth or community services platform designed for remote use — identifying which design decisions support access for users with limited digital literacy

modes.reason: Identifying UI elements across a range of apps (ordering, search, settings, navigation) builds the vocabulary students need to design with intent. Without having seen and named a range of element types, students default to what they know — typically a simple button grid — rather than selecting appropriate elements for the task.

nodes.label: Designing a user interface for an identified need
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design a user interface (on paper or digitally) that addresses an identified user need
criteria: Produces a labelled interface design showing key elements and layout
Explains how at least one design decision connects to the user's identified need

width.minimum: Produce a labelled sketch or digital mockup of a user interface for a specific purpose, showing the layout and key elements
width.typical: Design a user interface that addresses an identified need (from user stories); include layout, labels, navigation and key controls; explain how each design decision relates to what the user needs to do
wider: Design a user interface for the school canteen ordering app, then modify it for a user who is visually impaired — documenting changes to font size, colour contrast, and screen reader compatibility
Design a user interface intended for users from different cultural or language backgrounds — explaining how you used symbols, colour and layout to make it accessible across language differences

modes.reason: Students designing for themselves tend to produce interfaces that work for them but not for others. Designing for a specific, different user group (visually impaired, non-English speaking, remote community) makes the accessibility dimension concrete — it shifts design from personal preference to user-centred decision-making.

descriptors.title: Generate, modify and evaluate designs
descriptors.description: Generate, modify, communicate and evaluate designs
descriptors.knowledge: Students can generate, communicate and compare designs (AC9TDI4P03). They have produced and communicated design ideas and made comparisons. They have not yet formally evaluated designs against criteria or made and documented modifications to a preferred design based on evaluation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students generate a range of design ideas, evaluate them against design criteria and user stories, select a preferred design, and modify it where it does not satisfy all criteria.

nodes.label: Generating a range of design ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generate multiple distinct design ideas for a given problem rather than pursuing the first idea
criteria: Produces at least two design ideas that are meaningfully different
Each idea is represented clearly enough to be compared
nodes.hinge_reason: Genuine ideation in N1 is a prerequisite for evaluation in N2 — if students produce only one idea or near-identical variations, N2's comparative evaluation against criteria collapses into description. The evaluate step requires at least two meaningfully different options.

width.minimum: Generate at least two design ideas for the same problem that are genuinely different (not minor variations)
width.typical: Ideate a range of possible design solutions; represent each idea clearly enough that it can be compared to others; produce sketches, diagrams or descriptions for each
wider: Use a structured ideation method (e.g. sketching six thumbnails, mind-mapping from the user story) to generate ideas beyond the first obvious solution

Generate design ideas that each prioritise a different design criterion — e.g. one idea optimises for cost, another for accessibility, another for ease of use — making trade-offs explicit from the start

modes.reason: Students who default to their first idea lack ideation repertoire — they do not know how to generate alternatives. Accumulated experience with ideation methods (thumbnail sketches, constraint-flipping, stakeholder-first framing) builds the repertoire needed for genuine comparison.

nodes.label: Evaluating designs against criteria and user stories
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate design ideas against design criteria and user stories and identify which idea best meets them
criteria: References the design criteria and user stories when selecting a preferred design
Gives at least one criterion-based reason for the preference
nodes.hinge_reason: Criterion-based evaluation in N2 is prerequisite for N3's modification task — students who evaluate by preference rather than criteria cannot identify which criterion is unmet, so N3's 'modify to address the gap' has no gap to address.

width.minimum: Compare at least two design ideas against the design criteria and user stories; state which idea better satisfies them and give at least one reason
width.typical: Use the design criteria to systematically evaluate each idea (e.g. rate each against each criterion); identify a preferred design and explain which criteria it best satisfies and where it falls short
wider: Use a weighted decision matrix to evaluate designs where some criteria matter more than others — e.g. safety-critical criteria are non-negotiable, others are preferences
Include a user in the evaluation — explain each design to a peer acting as the user and record their responses as part of the evaluation

modes.reason: Students commonly select a preferred design based on personal preference and then justify it post-hoc rather than genuinely evaluating against criteria. The reasoning scaffold — apply criterion 1 to idea A and idea B, apply criterion 2, then decide — prevents preference-then-justify errors.

nodes.label: Modifying a design to meet unmet criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify where a preferred design does not satisfy a criterion or user story and propose a modification to address it
criteria: Identifies at least one gap between the preferred design and the criteria
Describes a modification that would address the identified gap

width.minimum: Identify at least one gap between the preferred design and the design criteria; describe a modification that would address the gap
width.typical: Review the preferred design against all criteria and user stories; document which criteria are met and which are not; propose modifications for unmet criteria and explain how each modification addresses the gap
wider: Modify a game or game controller design so it can be used by a wider range of players — documenting what the original design assumed about the user and how the modification removes that assumption
Prototype a modification and evaluate whether it resolves the gap — going through one iteration of the design-modify-evaluate cycle

modes.reason: Students tend to treat modification as correcting errors rather than genuinely extending the design to meet unmet criteria. Contexts where the unmet criterion is clear and consequential — a game that only some students can play, an interface that only English readers can navigate — make the modification purpose concrete.

descriptors.title: Implement programs with variables
descriptors.description: Implement algorithms as visual programs involving control structures, variables and input
descriptors.knowledge: Students can implement simple algorithms as visual programs involving control structures and input (AC9TDI4P04). They have written programs with basic sequences, simple branching, and loops in a visual environment. They have not yet used variables to store and reuse values, or combined variables with control structures to respond to user input.
descriptors.endpoint: Students implement algorithms as visual programs that use variables to store input, control structures (branching and iteration) to direct program flow, and produce correct output — verifying and fixing errors.

nodes.label: Using variables to store input
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a program that takes input from the user or environment, stores it in a variable, and uses the variable in later steps
criteria: Program stores a user input value in a named variable
The variable is used (not just stored) in a later step of the program
nodes.hinge_reason: Variable handling in N1 is prerequisite for N2 — programs combining variables with branches and loops require students to track how variable values change across iterations and affect branch conditions. Students who cannot use variables reliably cannot build the combined programs in N2.

width.minimum: Write a program that asks the user for one value, stores it in a variable, and uses that variable at least once later in the program
width.typical: Write programs that store user input in variables and use those variables in calculations, decisions, or output — e.g. ask how many shapes to draw, store in a variable, use that variable to control a loop count
wider: Write a program that takes input from the environment (e.g. a sensor value or a simulated tracker reading) and stores it in a variable — explaining the difference between user input and environmental input
Write a program with multiple variables that each store different pieces of information and interact in the algorithm — e.g. a score variable and a lives variable in a quiz

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse the variable name with its value, or overwrite a variable unintentionally. Programs where the variable's stored value visibly affects output in a meaningful way (number of shapes, score, direction) help students trace the variable's lifecycle from assignment to use.

nodes.label: Branching and iteration in programs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write programs that use branching to respond to different conditions and loops to repeat steps
criteria: Program includes at least one branch that produces different behaviour for different inputs
Program includes at least one loop with a clear termination condition
nodes.hinge_reason: N2's programs must exist and have observable behaviour before N3's verify-and-fix process can proceed — verification requires running a program and comparing actual to expected output. Students who cannot produce a program with branches and loops in N2 have nothing to test in N3.

width.minimum: Write a program with at least one branch (if/else) that produces different behaviour for different inputs, AND at least one loop that repeats steps a given number of times or until a condition is met
width.typical: Write programs that include multi-branch decisions (more than two alternatives), loops controlled by variable values, and combinations of both — e.g. an interactive quiz that checks answers (branching), gives feedback, updates the score (variable), and loops for each question
wider: Write a program that simulates automated ranger tasks — using iteration to repeat a monitoring loop and branching to select an action based on the detected condition (e.g. gate status, animal proximity)
Write a program with nested loops — repeating a shape a given number of times while shifting its position on each iteration (Turtle Graphics style)

modes.reason: Students who can write a loop or a branch in isolation often struggle to combine them. Programs with a clear, functional purpose — a quiz, a drawing pattern, a simulation — motivate the combination and make the program's behaviour verifiable by inspection.

This node integrates variables (Node 1), branching, and iteration into combined programs. The integration act is coordinating all three — variable value affects branch decision affects loop exit. Programs where the user can trace this chain during execution are the most effective contexts.

nodes.label: Verifying and fixing programs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can state expected program behaviour, test it by running the program, and fix errors when actual behaviour differs from expected
criteria: States the expected output before running the program
Identifies at least one discrepancy between expected and actual output and locates it in the code

width.minimum: State what the program should do for a specific input, run the program with that input, and identify whether the actual output matches — fix at least one error
width.typical: Test the program with multiple inputs including edge cases (e.g. exactly at a boundary condition); describe each error found, locate it in the code, and fix it; re-test after fixing
wider: Use systematic testing — a table of inputs and expected/actual outputs — to verify a program, including inputs that should trigger each branch and boundary values for loops
Diagnose and fix a provided program with a deliberate error — e.g. a direction is reversed, a condition is wrong — by reading the code before running it to predict the bug

modes.reason: Students typically run programs to find bugs rather than reasoning about what should happen first. Establishing the expected-then-actual routine (state expectation → run → compare → locate error) makes debugging a reasoning activity rather than a trial-and-error one.

descriptors.title: Evaluate solutions against criteria and community impact
descriptors.description: Evaluate existing and student solutions against the design criteria and user stories and their broader community impact
descriptors.knowledge: Students can discuss how existing and student solutions satisfy the design criteria and user stories (AC9TDI4P05). They have made comparisons between solutions and criteria. They have not yet evaluated broader community impact — the new demand is assessing solutions beyond their immediate function to consider effects on the wider community.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate solutions (their own and existing ones) against design criteria and user stories, and consider the broader community impact of those solutions.

nodes.label: Evaluating effectiveness against criteria and user stories
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how well a solution addresses the identified problem by testing it against the design criteria and user stories
criteria: References at least two design criteria or user story requirements in the evaluation
Provides evidence for whether each criterion is met
nodes.hinge_reason: The evaluation reasoning scaffold established in N1 (criterion → evidence → verdict) is applied in N2 (safety features) and N3 (community impact) — students who evaluate by description in N1 will describe rather than evaluate in the subsequent nodes.

width.minimum: Identify at least two criteria or user story requirements and state whether the solution meets each — with evidence
width.typical: Systematically evaluate a solution against all design criteria and user stories; for each criterion, provide evidence of whether it is met and explain what would need to change if it is not
wider: Evaluate the effectiveness of a student solution for a local interactive history walk — checking whether information is accurate, relevant to council needs, and accessible to expected visitors
Evaluate an existing solution (e.g. a community transport timetable system) against user stories for a specific group (e.g. elderly users, non-English speakers) rather than a general audience

modes.reason: Students typically describe a solution positively rather than testing it against criteria. The evaluation reasoning scaffold — criterion / evidence / met or not met / what would fix it — prevents description-as-evaluation and makes the claim-evidence structure explicit.

nodes.label: Evaluating safety features in existing solutions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how an existing solution provides safety tools and features, including for young people
criteria: Identifies at least one safety feature and names the risk it addresses
Explains who the safety feature is designed to protect

width.minimum: Identify at least one safety feature in an existing digital solution (e.g. a report/block button, age verification) and explain what risk it addresses
width.typical: Evaluate how an existing app or website provides safety features aligned with principles such as Safety by Design — identifying visible controls, reporting mechanisms, and privacy settings; explain what user group each feature protects and what gaps remain
wider: Compare the safety features of two apps used by the same age group — identifying where one provides stronger protections and explaining what the weaker app could add
Evaluate how AI-generated content is verified in a digital solution — testing whether the solution includes mechanisms for users to check factual accuracy against authoritative sources

modes.reason: Evaluating safety features across different apps and digital contexts helps students build a generalised framework for what 'safety by design' looks like — rather than memorising features of one specific app. AI content verification, reporting tools, and age controls each represent a different category of safety design that accumulates into a transferable evaluation lens.

nodes.label: Broader community impact
nodes.checkpoint: Students can consider the broader community impact of digital solutions beyond their immediate function
criteria: Identifies at least one community impact beyond whether the solution meets its immediate purpose
Connects the impact to a specific design decision or feature of the solution

width.minimum: Identify one positive and one potential negative community impact of a digital solution beyond whether it works as intended
width.typical: Evaluate an existing or student solution for its community impact — considering effects on different groups (e.g. those without access, those with privacy concerns, those whose data is collected); explain how design decisions contribute to these impacts
wider: Reflect on how community systems (transport timetables, licence databases, emergency alert systems) create dependencies — and what happens to people who cannot access or are excluded by those systems

Investigate how an AI-generated content issue (e.g. a biography with inaccurate information) could affect an individual's community reputation — evaluating the responsibility of the solution provider to prevent this

modes.reason: Community impact is abstract for students who think of digital solutions as tools rather than systems. Real-world contexts where impact is legible — a timetable that doesn't work for wheelchair users, an AI biography with errors about a real person — help students see that design decisions create winners and losers.

descriptors.title: Select tools for content creation
descriptors.description: Select and use appropriate digital tools effectively to create, locate and communicate content, applying common conventions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use the core features of common digital tools to create, locate and communicate content, following agreed conventions (AC9TDI4P06). They have used digital tools with provided guidance. They have not yet selected tools themselves — the shift is from using a nominated tool to choosing the appropriate one for a task.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select appropriate digital tools for creating, locating and communicating content, plan achievable steps and timeframes, apply common conventions, and judge the appropriateness of content for the audience.

nodes.label: Planning and selecting tools for a task
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan achievable steps and timeframes for a task and identify which digital tools are needed at each step
criteria: Lists steps for the task with realistic timeframes
Identifies at least one appropriate digital tool for each step with a reason

width.minimum: For a given task, list the steps needed and identify at least one digital tool for each step
width.typical: Create a plan with achievable steps and realistic timeframes for producing a digital solution; identify the specific tools needed for each stage (e.g. word processor for report, spreadsheet for data, presentation tool for communication); explain why each tool suits its step
wider: Plan a school recycling report that requires multiple tools at different stages — search tools for data, a spreadsheet for analysis, a word processor for writing, and a presentation tool for sharing — identifying where the output of one tool becomes the input of the next
Develop a plan for a collaborative spreadsheet to cost a school celebration — identifying which features (shared editing, formulas, tagging) make it the appropriate tool for this task

modes.reason: Tool selection is a reasoning task — students must work backwards from what the task requires to which tool's features match those requirements. Scaffolding the selection reasoning (what does this step produce? → what tool produces that format?) prevents students defaulting to the one tool they know.

nodes.label: Locating content effectively
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate relevant content using search engines and within documents by refining queries
criteria: Refines a search query at least once and explains what the refinement improved
Identifies at least one reason why a source may or may not be reliable

width.minimum: Perform a search, evaluate the results, and refine the query at least once to improve accuracy
width.typical: Locate content through search engines using effective query strategies — reviewing results, refining terms, using required search syntax; locate content within documents using find/search features; distinguish between more and less reliable sources
wider: Compare search results from two different queries on the same topic and explain why the refinement improved accuracy — identifying what the changed terms added or removed from the results
Verify AI-generated content about a local topic against an authoritative source — demonstrating the difference between locating information and accepting generated text as factually accurate

modes.reason: Students typically use the first search results they find and do not evaluate or refine. Seeing how the same question yields different quality results with different query strategies — and how AI-generated content can appear authoritative while being incorrect — builds the habit of verification rather than acceptance.

nodes.label: Judging appropriateness for audience and context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can judge whether content they have created or located is appropriate for the intended audience and purpose
criteria: Identifies the intended audience for the content
Gives at least one criterion-based reason for whether the content is appropriate for that audience

width.minimum: Review a piece of content (created or located) and explain whether it is appropriate for the intended audience — identifying at least one reason it is or is not suitable
width.typical: Apply multiple appropriateness criteria to content — is the tone right for the audience? Is the content accurate? Is the format suitable? Revise content where it does not meet these criteria
wider: Judge the tone of AI-generated text against the intended audience — deciding whether autocomplete or generative text is too formal, too informal, or inaccurate for the specific context and rewriting accordingly
Compare the same content created at different stages of an iterative process — explaining how teacher or peer feedback changed what was appropriate in subsequent versions

modes.reason: Students treat content as finished once produced. The judgement reasoning scaffold — audience / tone / accuracy / format / verdict — makes appropriateness a multi-dimensional check rather than a gut feel, and teaches revision as a response to evidence rather than preference.

descriptors.title: Collaborate and manage projects
descriptors.description: Select and use appropriate digital tools effectively to share content online, plan tasks and collaborate on projects, demonstrating agreed behaviours
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use the core features of common digital tools to share content, plan tasks and collaborate, following agreed rules (AC9TDI4P07). They have used shared tools with provided rules. They have not yet selected tools themselves or taken ownership of defining and moderating collaborative behaviours.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select appropriate tools for sharing content and project collaboration, manage files and project tasks, and demonstrate agreed online behaviours including cultural protocols and respect for others' work.

nodes.label: Organising and managing files for shared access
nodes.checkpoint: Students can organise and store shared files in a way that allows collaborators to locate and use them easily
criteria: Creates at least one folder with a logical sub-folder structure
Files are named consistently and can be located by purpose

width.minimum: Organise a set of project files using folders and consistent naming so that a collaborator can locate a specific file
width.typical: Create a folder structure for a project with logical hierarchy (e.g. main topic → sub-sections) and consistent file naming; explain the naming and organisation decisions in terms of how collaborators will access the files
wider: Design a folder structure for a school garden project with multiple teams — ensuring each team can find shared resources without access conflicts or confusion about which version is current
Compare two approaches to file organisation (flat folder with long filenames vs deep hierarchy with short names) and explain which is more effective for a given team size and project scope

modes.reason: File organisation is a habit-formation task — students understand the principle quickly but apply it inconsistently without deliberate practice. Consistency across multiple projects is more important than correctness on a single task.

nodes.label: Demonstrating agreed online behaviours
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define and follow agreed online community standards when collaborating in a digital environment
criteria: Identifies at least two agreed online behaviours with reasons
Demonstrates the behaviours in a collaborative task without being reminded

width.minimum: Identify at least two agreed behaviours for online collaboration (e.g. not deleting others' work, using appropriate language) and explain why each matters
width.typical: Define collective standards for an online collaboration, including appropriate language, not modifying others' work without permission, respecting intellectual property, and acknowledging sources; apply these consistently in a collaborative project
wider: Moderate language and behaviour in an online class forum — explaining the decisions made and connecting them to the agreed community standards
Apply cultural protocols when sharing images or information about First Nations Australians' cultural artefacts — identifying what permissions and attributions are required and why they matter

modes.reason: Agreed behaviours can feel abstract until students encounter a real breach. Contexts where the consequence of poor behaviour is visible — deleted work, inappropriate content in a shared document, cultural artefacts used without attribution — make the agreed standards meaningful rather than procedural.

nodes.label: Sharing content with stakeholders using appropriate tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and use an appropriate communication tool to share content with a specific stakeholder audience
criteria: Selects a tool appropriate for the specified audience and purpose
Shares content in a format the audience can access and engage with

width.minimum: Share a piece of project work with an audience beyond the class using a digital tool; explain why the tool chosen was appropriate for that audience
width.typical: Use a range of communication tools to share project content with different stakeholders (e.g. presenting to a parents and citizens meeting via online forum, reporting to a local council via email or document sharing); match the tool and format to the audience and purpose
wider: Present content for a school celebration to parents/guardians and school leadership via an online forum — adapting the format and tools to suit an audience that includes both technical and non-technical participants
Report findings about a local government issue (e.g. best location for a skate park) as a small group presentation — choosing tools that support group contribution and audience access

modes.reason: Students who have only shared work with peers struggle to adapt to a wider stakeholder audience. Presenting to a parents and citizens meeting or school leadership requires different tool choices, format decisions, and tone than classroom sharing — multiple audience contexts build this adaptability.

descriptors.title: Unique passphrases and password reuse risks
descriptors.description: Access multiple personal accounts using unique passphrases and explain the risks of password re-use
descriptors.knowledge: Students can access their school account using a memorised password and explain why it should be easy to remember but hard for others to guess (AC9TDI4P08). They have a single-account security practice. They have not yet managed multiple accounts with different credentials, or understood the specific risk cascade that password reuse creates.
descriptors.endpoint: Students access multiple accounts using unique passphrases and can explain why password reuse creates a risk cascade when one credential is compromised.

nodes.label: Why passphrases are stronger than passwords
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what makes a passphrase strong and why passphrases are more secure than short passwords
criteria: Explains at least two characteristics that make a passphrase strong
Contrasts a strong passphrase with a weak password example
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand what makes a credential strong cannot reason about the reuse risk in N2 — the cascade argument requires knowing that a compromised credential is now known to an attacker, and that requires understanding what 'compromised' means relative to credential strength.

width.minimum: Explain at least two characteristics of a strong passphrase (length, unpredictability) and contrast with a weak password
width.typical: Explain that passphrases are longer sequences of words that are hard to guess but easier to remember than short complex passwords; describe what makes a passphrase strong (length, not a famous phrase, not personal info) and what makes it weak
wider: Compare how a brute-force attack works against a short complex password versus a long passphrase — explaining why length is more protective than character complexity alone
Investigate how password managers store multiple unique passphrases securely — and why using a password manager is better than reusing a memorable password

modes.reason: The passphrase strength reasoning (length beats complexity; unpredictability beats memorability) is counter-intuitive. Students need the reasoning made explicit — 'a longer random phrase takes exponentially longer to guess than a short complex one' — before they can apply it to evaluate their own credentials.

nodes.label: The risk cascade of password reuse
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how reusing a password across multiple accounts creates a risk cascade when one account is compromised
criteria: Explains that a compromised password can be used to access other accounts if the same password is reused
Identifies at least two accounts where this compromise would matter

width.minimum: Describe a scenario where the same password is used on two accounts; explain what an attacker can do if they discover that password
width.typical: Explain the full risk cascade: one account is compromised → attacker obtains the password → attacker tries the same password on other accounts → multiple accounts compromised; identify which types of accounts are most valuable to protect (banking, school, personal communications)
wider: Explain how credential stuffing attacks work — automated attempts to use a leaked username/password list against multiple websites — and why unique passphrases prevent them
Investigate a real-world example where a social media breach led to bank or email account compromise because users had reused credentials — without identifying specific individuals

modes.reason: The password reuse risk is abstract until students see the chain: one compromise → many compromises. Multiple concrete scenarios (social media + school + gaming + banking) where each account has a different consequence of compromise help students understand what is at stake at each link in the chain.

descriptors.title: Digital footprint and privacy
descriptors.description: Explain the creation and permanence of their digital footprint and consider privacy when collecting user data
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify what personal data is stored and shared in their online accounts and discuss associated risks (AC9TDI4P09). They understand that accounts hold personal data. They have not yet understood the concept of digital footprint as cumulative and permanent, or considered data minimisation as a design principle when collecting user data.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how digital footprints are created and persist over time, and apply privacy considerations when thinking about collecting user data — including the principle of collecting only what is needed.

nodes.label: How digital footprints are created and persist
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how a digital footprint is created and why it persists over time
criteria: Describes at least one digital action and explains how it creates a persistent record
Explains why deleting a post may not remove the digital footprint it created
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand that digital footprints are permanent and cumulative cannot engage meaningfully with N2's data minimisation reasoning — the design principle of 'collect only what is needed' requires understanding why unnecessary data collection has lasting consequences.

width.minimum: Describe at least one scenario where a digital action creates a persistent record that could be resurfaced later
width.typical: Explain how online actions — comments, posts, images, search history — create records that persist and can be associated with a person later; describe at least two different ways a digital footprint is created and explain why deletion is not always effective
wider: Investigate how a comment made on a social media post or video links the commenter's identity to both the comment and the content — explaining why that association is permanent even if the post is later deleted
Explore how digital footprints accumulate over time — explaining that data from multiple platforms and years can be combined to build a detailed profile

modes.reason: Students tend to think of digital actions as ephemeral — 'I can just delete it'. Multiple contexts where deletion does not remove the trace (comment linked to another user's post, cached search results, data already shared with a third party) help students understand permanence as a structural feature, not a privacy setting.

nodes.label: Data minimisation — collecting only what is needed
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why collecting the minimum data needed for a purpose protects user privacy
criteria: Explains why collecting unnecessary data creates privacy risk
Identifies at least one example of unnecessary data collection and what could be collected instead

width.minimum: Give one example where collecting unnecessary personal data creates a privacy risk — and identify what could be collected instead
width.typical: Explain the principle that systems should collect the minimum data needed for their purpose; apply this to at least two scenarios — identifying what data is necessary, what is unnecessary, and what harm unnecessary collection creates
wider: Evaluate a sign-up form for an app and identify which fields are necessary for the stated purpose and which could be removed without affecting function — applying the data minimisation principle as a designer
Explain how collecting personal data to train generative AI models creates a long-term privacy risk — personal information shared once could surface in AI outputs far in the future

modes.reason: Students typically think of privacy as about keeping secrets, not about what should be collected in the first place. The data minimisation framing is counter-intuitive — it requires students to think as designers, not just users. Multiple scenarios (form design, AI training data) help students apply the principle from a design perspective rather than a personal-risk perspective.

descriptors.title: Acquire and validate data
descriptors.description: Acquire, store and validate data from a range of sources using software, including spreadsheets and databases
descriptors.knowledge: This is the first standard in the Managing Data sub-strand (begins at 7-8). Students bring general digital literacy from the Collaborating and Managing sub-strand and basic data representation understanding from the K strand. They have not yet formally acquired, stored or validated data using spreadsheets or databases.
descriptors.endpoint: Students acquire data from a range of sources to answer a specific question, store it using appropriate software (spreadsheets or databases), and validate the data by judging its relevance, correctness, currency and potential bias.

nodes.label: Defining a question that data can answer
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a question that requires data to answer and determine what data is needed
criteria: States a question that requires data to answer, not just opinion
Identifies at least one type of data needed to investigate the question
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot articulate what data is needed to answer their question will acquire irrelevant data or store data without purpose at Nodes 2 and 3. The question drives every subsequent phase — without a clear question, the data pipeline has no direction.

width.minimum: Given a scenario, state a question that data could help answer; identify what data would be needed to investigate it
width.typical: Frame a question for their own investigation; identify what data is needed, where it might come from, and what format it should be in
wider: Compare how the same broad question (e.g. 'Is the canteen selling the right food?') requires different data depending on how the question is framed — food preferences data vs nutritional data vs sales data
Limited width — question framing is a single skill. The breadth comes from the variety of investigations at later nodes, not from framing more questions.

modes.reason: Defining a researchable question requires students to reason from 'I want to know about X' to 'I need data of type Y from source Z to answer a specific question'. Without scaffolding this chain, students frame questions that cannot be answered with data — the question must precede and constrain every subsequent phase of the pipeline.

nodes.label: Acquiring data from sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can acquire data from a range of sources including surveys, existing datasets and digital platforms
criteria: Acquires data from at least one source relevant to the question
Records where the data came from

width.minimum: Acquire data from at least one source relevant to the question; record the source
width.typical: Acquire data from multiple sources (e.g. a survey they design and an existing dataset such as ABS); compare what each source provides
wider: Acquire and compare data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics to analyse geographic distribution of First Nations Australians, identifying past and emerging trends
Investigate how the source of data affects its reliability — compare self-reported survey data with independently measured data for the same question

modes.reason: Acquiring from multiple sources (survey + ABS) across different question types helps students see that source selection shapes what data is available — different sources answer different aspects of the same question. The width here is the variety of source types and their trade-offs.

nodes.label: Storing data appropriately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can store acquired data using software appropriate for how it will be accessed and analysed
criteria: Stores data in an organised format with appropriate headers or field names
Data is accessible for the intended analysis (not locked in an unusable format)

width.minimum: Store data in a spreadsheet or database; organise it with appropriate column headers or fields
width.typical: Choose between a spreadsheet and a database based on how the data will be used (visualisation vs filtering/querying); justify the choice
wider: Limited width — storage is a technical decision with a small number of valid options at this level (spreadsheet vs database). The genuine breadth is in the variety of data and questions, which is captured at other nodes.

nodes.label: Validating data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can validate data by judging its relevance, correctness, currency and potential bias
criteria: Identifies at least one data quality issue (relevance, correctness, currency or bias)
Explains why the issue matters for answering the question

width.minimum: Given a dataset, identify at least one issue with relevance, correctness or currency; explain why it matters for the question being investigated
width.typical: Apply multiple validation checks — is the data relevant to the question? Is it correct? Is it current? Is the sample representative? Identify and explain at least two issues
wider: Evaluate how training data bias affects AI model output — what happens when a model is trained on data from a single demographic group?
Compare data quality across multiple sources for the same question — which source is more reliable and why?

modes.reason: Validation is where students encounter the hardest thinking — judging relevance, correctness, currency and bias requires applying multiple criteria to the same data. Seeing different data quality problems across multiple datasets (ABS, surveys, AI training data) helps students build the validation habit rather than checking one criterion in one scenario.

descriptors.title: Analyse and visualise data
descriptors.description: Analyse and visualise data using a range of software, including spreadsheets and databases, to draw conclusions and make predictions by identifying trends
descriptors.knowledge: Students can acquire, store and validate data from a range of sources (AC9TDI8P01). They have worked with data in spreadsheets but have not yet selected visualisation types, summarised data by attributes to identify trends, or drawn evidence-based conclusions and predictions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and visualise data by choosing appropriate graph types and representations, summarise data by attributes to identify trends and patterns, and draw conclusions and make predictions supported by evidence from the data.

nodes.label: Choosing visualisation types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select an appropriate visualisation type (graph, chart, map, diagram) for a given dataset and explain why it suits the data
criteria: Selects a visualisation type that is appropriate for the data structure (not just defaulting to one type)
Explains why the chosen type suits this particular dataset
nodes.hinge_reason: Students with only one or two graph types in their repertoire will default to the same type regardless of data structure. Nodes 2 and 3 require students to choose visualisations that reveal the relevant patterns — a thin repertoire produces graphs that obscure the trends they need to identify and conclude from.

width.minimum: Given a dataset, choose a graph type and explain why it is appropriate for showing the pattern or relationship in the data
width.typical: Compare visualisation options for multidimensional data — explain why a scatter plot coloured by a third variable reveals more than a simple bar chart for the same data
wider: Investigate how visualisation choices can reveal or obscure patterns — compare two different graph types for the same dataset and explain what each makes visible and what it hides
Explore how social network diagrams or geographic maps reveal patterns that standard graphs cannot

modes.reason: Visualisation selection requires accumulating a repertoire of graph types and understanding what each makes visible. Students need enough examples to stop defaulting to bar charts — the repertoire is the prior condition for choosing appropriately.

nodes.label: Identifying trends and patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can summarise data by attributes to identify trends, patterns and outliers
criteria: Identifies at least one trend or pattern in the data
Describes the trend in context (not just 'it goes up')

width.minimum: Identify at least one trend or pattern in a visualised dataset; describe what the trend shows
width.typical: Summarise data by sorting or grouping by attributes; identify trends and at least one outlier; explain what the pattern means in context
wider: Compare trends identified manually with those generated by an AI model using natural language queries — do they find the same patterns?
Investigate how sorting crime data by type of offence reveals trends that raw data obscures

nodes.label: Drawing conclusions and making predictions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw evidence-based conclusions from analysed data and make predictions by extending identified trends
criteria: States a conclusion that references specific evidence from the data
Makes a prediction that extends an identified trend
Does not present opinion as conclusion — the conclusion follows from the data

width.minimum: State a conclusion supported by at least one piece of evidence from the data; make one prediction based on an identified trend
width.typical: Draw conclusions that reference multiple data points or patterns; make predictions and explain the reasoning; acknowledge limitations or uncertainty in the prediction
wider: Compare a predictive AI model's output against manually tagged data to evaluate its accuracy and effectiveness
Evaluate the confidence of a prediction — what would need to be true for the prediction to hold, and what could invalidate it?

modes.reason: Drawing conclusions requires students to distinguish between what the data shows, what it suggests, and what is uncertain. Scaffolding the reasoning structure (evidence → conclusion → prediction → limitation) prevents students from presenting opinion as data-supported conclusion.

Conclusions integrate visualisation selection (Node 1) and trend identification (Node 2) into evidence-based claims. Students who treat conclusion-drawing as separate from the prior analysis produce unsupported claims.

descriptors.title: Model structured data
descriptors.description: Model and query the attributes of objects and events using structured data
descriptors.knowledge: This is the first standard in the Modelling Data sub-strand (begins at 7-8). Students have used spreadsheets to store and organise data (AC9TDI8P01) but have not yet modelled objects and events as structured data with defined attributes, nor queried data using filtering, sorting or SQL.
descriptors.endpoint: Students model objects and events as structured data by identifying relevant attributes and appropriate formats, and query the data using filtering, sorting and simple SQL (SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY) to answer questions.

nodes.label: What structured data is
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that structured data represents objects or events as records with defined attributes, and identify what attributes are relevant for a given purpose
criteria: Identifies at least three relevant attributes for a given object or event
Explains why each attribute is relevant to the purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify relevant attributes for a given purpose will create tables at Node 2 with missing, irrelevant or incorrectly formatted fields. Poorly structured tables cannot be queried meaningfully at Node 3 — the data model shapes every query.

width.minimum: Given an object or event, name at least three attributes that describe it; explain why the chosen attributes are relevant to the task
width.typical: Model objects and events from a real scenario (e.g. canteen products with name, price, quantity, nutritional value); choose appropriate data formats for each attribute (text, number, date)
wider: Design a database schema for a real-world context and justify why each attribute was included and what was excluded
Compare how the same event (e.g. a sports match) would be modelled differently for different purposes (scheduling vs statistics vs commentary)

modes.reason: Selecting relevant attributes requires students to reason from purpose: what question are we answering? → what information does the query need? → which attributes capture that information? Students who list attributes without connecting them to purpose create tables that cannot answer the intended question when queried at Node 3.

nodes.label: Storing structured data in tables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create a spreadsheet table or database table that correctly stores structured data with appropriate column formats
criteria: Creates a table with named columns and correctly formatted data
Data entries are consistent within each column
nodes.hinge_reason: Inconsistent column formats (text in number columns, mixed date formats) break SQL queries at Node 3. Students who produce tables with formatting errors cannot write meaningful queries against their own data — the table quality gates the querying phase.

width.minimum: Create a table with named columns and at least 5 records; use appropriate formats (text, number, date) for each column
width.typical: Create a table with consistent formatting; identify and correct data entry errors (e.g. text in a number column, inconsistent date formats); explain why consistent formatting matters for querying
wider: Limited width — table creation is a mechanical skill at this level. The genuine breadth is in what is modelled (captured at Node 1) and how it is queried (captured at Node 3).

modes.reason: Table creation with consistent formatting is a precision skill — inconsistent data types within a column break querying. Width is thin. What helps is more practice creating tables for different real-world objects until correct formatting is automatic.

nodes.label: Querying data to answer questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can filter, sort and query structured data to answer specific questions, including using simple SQL
criteria: Filters or sorts data to produce a result that answers the given question
Explains what the query result shows in context

width.minimum: Filter or sort a table to answer a given question; explain what the result shows
width.typical: Write simple SQL queries using SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY to answer questions from a database; compare the result of different queries on the same data
wider: Investigate how query design affects what patterns are visible — compare two queries on the same dataset that reveal different insights
Explore how structured data modelling underpins a real application (e.g. a library catalogue, a booking system, a historical events database)

modes.reason: SQL query writing requires students to translate a question into a formal instruction with exact syntax. Scaffolding the translation (what do I want to find? → which column? → which condition? → what order?) prevents students from trial-and-erroring rather than reasoning about what the query should do.

descriptors.title: Decompose real-world problems
descriptors.description: Define and decompose real-world problems with design criteria and by creating user stories
descriptors.knowledge: Students can define problems using given or co-developed design criteria and independently created user stories (AC9TDI6P01). They have not yet decomposed complex real-world problems into sub-problems or justified their decomposition decisions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students define real-world problems by framing what is known and what outcome is desired, decompose them into manageable sub-problems, and create user stories that capture user needs to guide the design process.

nodes.label: Framing a problem
nodes.checkpoint: Students can frame a real-world problem in terms of what is known, why it is important, and what outcome is desired
criteria: States what is known about the problem clearly
Explains why the problem matters
Describes what a successful outcome looks like
nodes.hinge_reason: In a Mode B design cycle, every downstream phase (decomposition, user stories, design, evaluation) flows from the problem frame. A weak or absent frame produces decompositions that solve the wrong problem, user stories that don't connect to a defined need, and designs that cannot be evaluated against criteria.

width.minimum: Given a real-world scenario, state what is known, why the problem matters, and what a successful outcome looks like
width.typical: Frame a problem from a scenario that has multiple possible interpretations; justify why the chosen framing matters for the direction of the solution
wider: Apply problem framing to a context sourced from a First Nations community — how does the community's perspective shape what the problem actually is?
Investigate how problem framing affects solution direction — frame the same scenario two different ways and predict how each framing leads to a different solution

modes.reason: Problem framing requires students to make explicit what is known, why it matters, and what success looks like — three distinct questions that students commonly conflate or skip. Scaffolding the framing structure prevents students from jumping to solutions before the problem is defined.

nodes.label: Decomposing into sub-problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can break a defined problem into manageable parts by asking a series of questions and sub-questions
criteria: Identifies at least three sub-problems from a defined problem
Explains how each sub-problem contributes to solving the whole

width.minimum: Given a defined problem, identify at least three sub-problems and explain how each contributes to the whole
width.typical: Decompose a problem into sub-problems with dependencies identified — which parts need to be solved before others; justify why the chosen decomposition is appropriate
wider: Use AI tools to assist decomposition of a problem and critically evaluate whether the AI's breakdown matches the problem framing — what did it miss or misinterpret?

Limited width — decomposition as a skill does not vary dramatically across problem contexts. The same questioning technique (what do we need to know? what depends on what?) applies regardless of domain.

nodes.label: Creating user stories
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create user stories that capture user needs and use them as design criteria to guide the solution
criteria: Writes user stories in a recognisable format that captures user, goal and reason
Connects each user story to a specific sub-problem or design criterion

width.minimum: Write at least two user stories in the standard format (As a [user], I want [goal], so that [reason]); connect each to a sub-problem from Node 2
width.typical: Write user stories for different user types within the same problem; identify where user needs conflict and explain how design criteria help prioritise
wider: Create user stories from direct stakeholder input — interview a real user or community member and translate their needs into stories
Evaluate whether AI-generated user stories accurately capture user needs or introduce assumptions not present in the original problem framing

modes.reason: User stories integrate problem framing (Node 1) and decomposition (Node 2) by translating sub-problems into user-centred requirements. Students who write user stories without connecting them to their decomposition are completing a format exercise, not using stories as a design tool.

descriptors.title: Design nested algorithms
descriptors.description: Design algorithms involving nested control structures and represent them using flowcharts and pseudocode
descriptors.knowledge: Students can design algorithms involving multiple branching alternatives and iteration (AC9TDI6P02). They can use sequence, branching and iteration as separate control structures. They have not yet nested control structures inside each other or represented algorithms in both flowcharts and pseudocode.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design algorithms involving nested control structures (IF inside IF, IF inside loops, loops inside loops), represent them precisely using both flowcharts and pseudocode, and explain the design decisions at each branching or iteration point.

nodes.label: Control structures as building blocks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify sequence, branching and iteration as distinct control structures and explain what each does
criteria: Names sequence, branching and iteration correctly
Identifies which structure is used in a given simple algorithm
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reliably identify sequence, branching and iteration as distinct structures cannot understand what it means to put one inside another at Node 2. Nesting requires a clear mental model of what is outer and what is inner — this requires the structures to be individually identifiable first.

width.minimum: Name the three control structures (sequence, branching, iteration); given a simple algorithm, identify which structure is being used
width.typical: Identify control structures in multiple algorithm examples; explain when each is appropriate — branching for decisions, iteration for repetition
wider: Limited width — the three control structures are a fixed set. More examples reinforce recognition but do not broaden the concept. The genuine breadth comes from how they are combined at later nodes.

modes.reason: The three control structures must be reliably identified before students can understand how they combine. More algorithm examples at this node builds recognition fluency — the prerequisite for understanding what nesting adds at Node 2.

nodes.label: What nesting means
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what it means to nest one control structure inside another and why nesting is useful for more complex decisions
criteria: Identifies the outer and inner structures in a nested algorithm
Explains what the nesting achieves that a flat structure cannot
Does not confuse nesting with sequential ordering of separate structures
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot articulate what nesting achieves that a flat structure cannot will produce flat algorithms at Node 3 when problems require nested logic. They will either avoid nesting (producing incorrect algorithms) or apply it randomly (producing non-functional ones).

width.minimum: Given a nested algorithm example (e.g. IF inside IF), identify the outer and inner structures; explain what the nesting achieves that a flat structure cannot
width.typical: Identify nesting in multiple examples (IF inside IF, IF inside loop, loop inside loop); explain why each nesting pattern is useful for its specific problem
wider: Limited width — nesting is a single conceptual insight (a structure inside a structure). More nesting patterns extend the concept but the core understanding is the same.

modes.reason: Students who don't grasp that nesting creates a hierarchy of decisions produce flat algorithms that cannot handle complex logic. Seeing different nesting patterns (IF inside IF, IF inside loop, loop inside loop) across different problem contexts is the width that builds robust understanding.

nodes.label: Designing nested algorithms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design an algorithm with nested control structures to solve a problem, making deliberate choices about what to nest and why
criteria: Designs an algorithm with at least one correctly nested structure
Represents the algorithm in at least one notation (flowchart or pseudocode)
The nesting solves the problem — removing it would break the algorithm

width.minimum: Design an algorithm with at least one nested structure (e.g. IF inside a loop) to solve a given problem; represent it in either flowchart or pseudocode
width.typical: Design algorithms for problems requiring different nesting patterns; represent in both flowchart and pseudocode; explain design decisions at each branching point
wider: Design algorithms for real-world contexts such as currency calculation or change-giving, where nesting handles multiple denominations
Modify an existing algorithm to fix an error or change functionality — identify how the nesting structure needs to change

modes.reason: Designing nested algorithms for different real-world contexts (currency, change-giving, rule-checking) helps students see that nesting emerges from problem complexity, not from the algorithm designer's preference. More problem contexts = more robust understanding of why nesting is necessary.

nodes.label: Representing in flowcharts and pseudocode
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent the same nested algorithm precisely in both flowchart and pseudocode notation, and translate between them
criteria: Produces both a flowchart and pseudocode for the same algorithm
Both representations produce the same output for the same input

width.minimum: Given an algorithm in one notation, represent it in the other; verify that both representations produce the same output
width.typical: Represent a self-designed algorithm in both notations; annotate the pseudocode with comments explaining design decisions; identify where each notation is clearer
wider: Evaluate whether a design could be simplified without losing functionality — use the dual representation to spot redundant nesting
Limited width — flowcharts and pseudocode are two notations for the same thing. The breadth comes from the variety of algorithms represented, which is captured at Node 3.

modes.reason: Translating between flowchart and pseudocode is a precision skill requiring fluency with both notations. Width is thin — the same translation process applies regardless of algorithm. Practice with more algorithms builds the dual-representation habit.

descriptors.title: Trace algorithms for errors
descriptors.description: Trace algorithms to predict output for a given input and to identify errors
descriptors.knowledge: Students can design algorithms with nested control structures and represent them in flowcharts and pseudocode (AC9TDI8P05). They can follow simple algorithms but have not yet systematically traced algorithms using desk checks, specified test cases with expected outputs, or identified errors through tracing.
descriptors.endpoint: Students trace algorithms step by step to predict output for given inputs, specify test cases with expected and actual outputs, and identify and explain errors found through systematic tracing.

nodes.label: Tracing step by step
nodes.checkpoint: Students can trace an algorithm precisely, step by step, tracking variable values to predict the output for a given input
criteria: Traces each step in order without skipping
Correctly tracks variable values through the algorithm
Predicts the final output accurately for the given input
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who skip steps or track variable values loosely cannot identify errors at Node 3 — they will trace incorrectly and miss the divergence between expected and actual output. Imprecise tracing makes test case specification at Node 2 meaningless.

width.minimum: Given an algorithm and an input, trace through each step and predict the output
width.typical: Use a desk check table (input, variables, output) to trace an algorithm systematically; track how variable values change at each step
wider: Follow instructions for making woven baskets or nets by hand, as done by First Nations Australians, and trace the steps to predict how modifications to the instructions would change the output
Limited width — tracing is a mechanical process applied the same way regardless of algorithm. More algorithms to trace is practice, not broader application.

modes.reason: Systematic tracing is the prerequisite for specifying test cases and identifying errors. Width is thin — tracing works the same way regardless of algorithm. What helps is more practice: more algorithms traced precisely, building the discipline of step-by-step tracking until it becomes habitual.

nodes.label: Specifying test cases
nodes.checkpoint: Students can specify test cases by choosing inputs and stating expected outputs before tracing
criteria: Specifies at least one test case with input and expected output before tracing
Compares expected output against actual output after tracing

width.minimum: Given an algorithm, specify at least one test case with a chosen input and the expected output; trace to check whether actual output matches
width.typical: Specify multiple test cases including edge cases (boundary values, zero, negative); explain why each test case was chosen and what it tests
wider: Evaluate how test case selection affects confidence in algorithm correctness — can three test cases be enough, or does the algorithm's structure determine how many are needed?
Limited width — test case specification is a systematic skill. The variety comes from the algorithms being tested, not from the testing process itself.

modes.reason: Specifying test cases requires students to reason about what the algorithm should do before they trace it — stating expected outputs requires understanding the algorithm's intent. Scaffolding the reasoning (what should happen at this input? why? what would an edge case expose?) prevents students from specifying tests that only confirm correct behaviour.

nodes.label: Identifying and explaining errors
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify errors in an algorithm by comparing expected and actual outputs, and explain what caused the error
criteria: Identifies the location of an error through systematic tracing
Explains what the error is (not just that the output is wrong)

width.minimum: Given an algorithm that contains an error, trace it to find where the output diverges from the expected result; state what the error is
width.typical: Identify errors through tracing; explain the cause of each error (e.g. wrong comparison operator, loop termination off by one); suggest a correction
