wider: Investigate how automated testing tools extend manual tracing — what do they catch that manual tracing might miss?
Debug an algorithm with multiple interacting errors — trace to isolate each error independently

modes.reason: Identifying errors across algorithms with different error types (wrong comparison, off-by-one, misplaced logic) builds the pattern-recognition needed for systematic debugging. Each error type is a distinct diagnostic context — breadth here is breadth of error patterns encountered.

descriptors.title: Design user experience
descriptors.description: Design the user experience of a digital system
descriptors.knowledge: Students can design a user interface for a digital system (AC9TDI6P03) and generate, modify, communicate and evaluate design ideas (AC9TDI6P04). They have experience designing interfaces but have not yet considered user experience holistically — including branding, user values, and how design decisions serve user stories.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design the user experience of a digital system by creating wireframes and storyboards across multiple pages, applying branding guidelines for visual identity, and justifying design decisions against user stories and design criteria.

nodes.label: UX vs UI
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish user experience from user interface and explain that UX design centres on how users interact with and feel about a system, not just how it looks
criteria: Correctly identifies UX and UI decisions in a given example
Explains that UX includes flow, ease of use, and user satisfaction — not just visual design
Does not treat UX and UI as interchangeable
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat UX and UI as interchangeable will produce wireframes that only address layout without considering user flow or satisfaction at Nodes 3 and 5. The UX/UI distinction shapes every design justification in this standard.

width.minimum: Given examples, identify which design decisions are about user experience (flow, ease of use, satisfaction) and which are about user interface (layout, colour, buttons)
width.typical: Analyse an existing digital system — identify UX decisions and UI decisions separately; explain how a good UI can still have poor UX and vice versa
wider: Compare the UX of the same service across different platforms (e.g. mobile app vs website vs voice assistant) — how does the experience change when the interface changes?
Limited width — the UX/UI distinction is a single conceptual insight. More examples reinforce but do not meaningfully broaden the understanding.

modes.reason: The UX/UI distinction is a misconception-prone conceptual boundary — students who conflate them will produce wireframes treated as complete UX designs. Seeing the distinction applied across multiple platforms (mobile, web, voice) resolves the misconception more reliably than a single definition.

nodes.label: Users and their needs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what user stories and design criteria capture and how they guide design decisions
criteria: Identifies the user need captured in a given user story
Explains how a specific design decision serves or fails a user story
Identifies at least one case where different users would need different design choices

width.minimum: Given a user story, identify what the user needs and what the design must satisfy to meet that need
width.typical: Compare two different user stories for the same product; explain how design decisions would differ to serve each user
wider: Consider why a user might choose a product beyond utility — how brand alignment with user values and identity contributes to appeal
Evaluate accessibility considerations — how design criteria change when designing for users with diverse needs

modes.reason: User stories for different user types (different demographics, accessibility needs, values) reveal that design criteria vary with user context. Students who only work with one user type don't see how design decisions must trade off between competing user needs.

nodes.label: Wireframes and storyboards
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use wireframes and storyboards to plan and communicate the user experience across multiple pages or screens of a digital system
criteria: Produces wireframes showing layout and navigation for at least two connected pages
Shows how a user moves between the pages

width.minimum: Sketch a wireframe for at least two connected pages of a digital system; show how a user navigates between them
width.typical: Create wireframes and a storyboard that maps the user journey across multiple pages; annotate design decisions with references to user stories
wider: Compare wireframes at different fidelity levels (sketch vs digital tool) and explain when each is appropriate in the design process

Limited width — wireframing is a technique. More pages or more detail is practice volume, not broader application. The genuine breadth is in the variety of user journeys the wireframes serve, which is captured through user stories at Node 2.

modes.reason: Wireframing is a practical skill that requires building comfort with visual layout conventions — what to show, what to annotate, how to indicate navigation. More wireframing practice is more useful than varying the type of application being wireframed.

nodes.label: Branding and visual identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply basic branding guidelines (colours, styling, typography) to communicate a consistent visual identity that supports the user experience
criteria: Applies consistent colours and styling across wireframes
Explains how visual choices communicate the product's identity or values
Branding supports rather than contradicts the user experience

width.minimum: Apply a consistent colour palette and styling across wireframes; explain how visual choices communicate the product's identity
width.typical: Create simple branding guidelines (colour palette, typography, tone) for a product; apply them across wireframes and explain how they support the user experience
wider: Investigate how brand alignment with user values affects product appeal beyond utility — why users choose products that reflect their identity
Compare the evolution of a real interface's branding over time (e.g. search engines, social media) and explain what drove the design shifts

nodes.label: Design a complete user experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design a complete user experience that integrates wireframes, storyboards, branding, and user stories into a cohesive design justified against design criteria
criteria: Produces a cohesive UX design that includes wireframes, branding and user stories
Justifies at least two design decisions against user stories or design criteria
Design is internally consistent — branding, layout and navigation work together

width.minimum: Produce a UX design for a digital system with wireframes, branding and at least one user story; justify at least one design decision against the criteria
width.typical: Produce a complete UX design with multiple wireframes, a storyboard, branding guidelines, and user stories; justify key design decisions and identify where trade-offs were made between competing user needs
wider: Present the design to peers or stakeholders and iterate based on feedback — demonstrate how the design changed in response to evaluation
Evaluate the design against accessibility criteria not originally in the brief — what would need to change to serve a broader user base?

modes.reason: This node synthesises all preceding UX components — UX/UI understanding, user stories, wireframes and branding — into a single coherent design. Students who have learned each component separately commonly produce designs where branding and wireframes don't serve the user stories. The integration task surfaces whether the components were genuinely connected throughout.

descriptors.title: Generate and evaluate designs
descriptors.description: Generate, modify, communicate and evaluate alternative designs
descriptors.knowledge: Students can generate, modify, communicate and evaluate design ideas (AC9TDI6P04). They have experience producing and sharing designs but have not yet systematically generated alternatives, used iterative modification, or evaluated designs against user stories for diverse users.
descriptors.endpoint: Students generate multiple alternative designs using appropriate tools (concept maps, wireframes, diagrams, AI), communicate design ideas clearly, modify a preferred design iteratively based on evaluation, and evaluate alternatives against design criteria and user stories.

nodes.label: Generating alternative designs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use strategies to generate multiple alternative design ideas rather than committing to a single idea
criteria: Produces at least two genuinely different design alternatives for the same brief
Communicates each design clearly enough for someone else to understand the idea
Explains why generating alternatives is valuable before selecting one
nodes.hinge_reason: Students with only one generation strategy produce variants of the same idea rather than genuine alternatives. Node 2 evaluation requires meaningfully different designs to evaluate — if all designs are the same idea with surface variation, the evaluation at Node 2 has nothing to compare.

width.minimum: Generate at least two alternative designs for a given brief; communicate each using sketches, diagrams or digital tools
width.typical: Use multiple generation strategies (brainstorming, sketching, concept mapping) to produce alternatives; explain why generating multiple options before committing leads to better outcomes
wider: Use generative AI to produce multiple design prototypes and compare them against user needs — evaluate what the AI generated well and what it missed
Research how professional design teams use divergent thinking techniques to generate alternatives before converging on a solution

modes.reason: Alternative generation requires students to resist committing to the first idea — the repertoire of generation strategies (brainstorming, sketching, concept mapping) is what enables genuine alternatives. More strategies practised = less likely to produce variants of the same idea.

nodes.label: Evaluating against criteria and user stories
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate alternative designs against design criteria and user stories, identifying strengths and weaknesses of each
criteria: Compares designs against specific criteria rather than personal preference
Identifies at least one strength and one weakness per design
References user stories when explaining why a design succeeds or fails

width.minimum: Compare two designs against given design criteria; identify which better satisfies a user story and explain why
width.typical: Evaluate multiple designs against criteria and user stories including the needs of diverse users; identify trade-offs where a design serves one user well but another poorly
wider: Evaluate how design decisions affect diverse user groups — accessibility, cultural context, language
Assess a real commercial product against its likely design criteria and user stories — what trade-offs did the designers make?

modes.reason: Students who cannot articulate why one design is better than another will modify designs randomly rather than purposefully. Evaluating different designs against different criteria and different user stories is genuine breadth that builds the evaluative skill.

nodes.label: Iterative modification
nodes.checkpoint: Students can modify a preferred design iteratively based on evaluation feedback, documenting what changed and why
criteria: Modifies a design in response to specific evaluation feedback
Documents what changed between versions
Explains how each modification improves the design against criteria or user stories

width.minimum: Modify a design in response to evaluation; explain what was changed and how the modification improves the design against criteria
width.typical: Complete at least two rounds of modification based on feedback (peer review, user testing, or self-evaluation against criteria); document each modification and its rationale
wider: Limited width — iterative modification is a process that operates the same way regardless of design context. The variation lies in what is being modified (captured in the design brief) not in how iteration works. More iterations are practice, not broader application.

descriptors.title: Implement programs with functions
descriptors.description: Implement, modify and debug programs involving control structures and functions in a general-purpose programming language
descriptors.knowledge: Students can implement algorithms as visual programs involving control structures, variables and input (AC9TDI6P05). They have programmed in visual/block-based environments but have not yet used a general-purpose text-based language, defined functions, or systematically debugged programs.
descriptors.endpoint: Students implement working programs in a general-purpose language (e.g. Python, JavaScript) using branching, iteration, variables and functions; read and modify existing code to change functionality; and debug programs by identifying and fixing errors.

nodes.label: Writing programs with control structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write programs in a general-purpose language using branching, iteration and variables to solve problems
criteria: Writes a program that runs without syntax errors
Program uses at least one branching structure and one loop
Variables are used to store and manipulate data
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot write syntactically correct programs in a text-based language cannot define or call functions (Node 2), read and modify existing code (Node 3), or debug programs (Node 4). Syntax errors block all subsequent production skills in this standard.

width.minimum: Write a program that uses at least one branching structure and one loop with variables to solve a given problem
width.typical: Write programs using nested control structures (IF inside loops, loops with conditionals) to solve more complex problems; use meaningful variable names and comments
wider: Write a program that receives data from the environment to change behaviour (e.g. reading moisture from a soil sensor to control a watering system)
Apply programming to an open-ended student-chosen problem with self-selected context

modes.reason: The transition from visual/block-based to text-based programming requires building syntax fluency. Width is thin — Python syntax doesn't vary across contexts. What helps is more practice: writing more small programs, fixing more syntax errors, building comfort with the text environment.

nodes.label: Defining and using functions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define functions that accept arguments and produce output, and use them to organise programs into reusable parts
criteria: Defines a function that accepts at least one argument
The function produces output that varies based on the argument
Calls the function correctly from the main program

width.minimum: Define a function that takes at least one argument and returns or produces output; call the function from the main program
width.typical: Define and use multiple functions that produce different output based on their arguments; explain why functions make programs easier to read and maintain
wider: Refactor an existing program by extracting repeated code into functions — explain how the refactored version is easier to modify
Limited width — function definition is a mechanical programming skill. The breadth comes from the variety of problems they solve, which is captured at Node 1 and Node 3.

nodes.label: Reading and modifying existing code
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and interpret an existing program, explain what it does, and modify the code to change its functionality
criteria: Explains what an existing program does in plain language
Makes a modification that changes the program's behaviour as intended

width.minimum: Given an existing program, explain what it does; make one modification to change its behaviour and verify the change works
width.typical: Read an unfamiliar program (e.g. a weather app showing temperatures); modify it to add functionality (e.g. include rainfall, UV levels); explain what each modification changes
wider: Use AI tools to generate code for a given problem; critically evaluate the generated code for correctness, efficiency and readability before using it
Read and modify a program written by a peer — identify what they did well and suggest improvements

modes.reason: Reading and modifying code in different domains (weather apps, data tools, games) builds the transferable reading skill — students who only read code they wrote cannot interpret unfamiliar structure. Variety of program contexts is genuine breadth here.

nodes.label: Debugging programs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and fix errors in programs by testing, reading error messages, and tracing program execution
criteria: Identifies the location and type of error in a program
Fixes the error so the program produces the intended output
Explains what was wrong and why the fix works

width.minimum: Given a program with an error, identify the error and fix it; explain what was wrong
width.typical: Debug programs with multiple errors (syntax and logic); use error messages and systematic testing to locate each error; explain the fix for each
wider: Compare debugging strategies — reading error messages vs adding print statements vs using a step-through debugger; explain when each is most useful
Limited width — debugging is a process applied the same way regardless of program. The variety comes from the programs being debugged, not from the debugging process itself.

modes.reason: Debugging requires a systematic process — read the error message → locate the relevant code → understand what it's trying to do → identify what's wrong → fix and verify. Students who approach debugging by random modification or by re-reading code without a strategy waste time and miss logic errors. Scaffolding the debugging process builds a transferable systematic habit.

descriptors.title: Evaluate against future impact
descriptors.description: Evaluate existing and student solutions against the design criteria, user stories and possible future impact
descriptors.knowledge: Students can evaluate solutions against design criteria, user stories and broader community impact (AC9TDI6P06). They have evaluated whether solutions meet criteria, but have not yet considered possible future impact across economic, environmental, or social dimensions, or evaluated for safety and misinformation risks.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate existing and student solutions against design criteria and user stories, and analyse the possible future impact of solutions across economic, environmental and social dimensions, including safety, misinformation and sustainability considerations.

nodes.label: Evaluating existing solutions against criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate existing digital solutions against design criteria and user stories to inform their own design decisions.
criteria: Evaluates an existing solution against specific criteria rather than personal preference
Identifies whether each criterion is met, partially met or unmet with evidence
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot evaluate evidence against criteria in a structured way cannot perform impact analysis at Nodes 2–3 — both require the same judgement pattern (evidence → assessment → implication). Evaluation of their own solution at Node 4 also directly depends on this skill.

width.minimum: Evaluate a given existing solution against at least two design criteria and one user story; state whether each is met and explain why.
width.typical: Evaluate a solution against multiple criteria and user stories; distinguish between fully met, partially met and unmet requirements; suggest specific improvements for unmet requirements
wider: Evaluate a real commercial platform against Safety by Design principles for young people — are privacy settings comprehensive, easy to use, and set to maximum protection by default?

Limited width — evaluation against criteria is a consistent analytical process. More criteria or more solutions is practice, not broader application. The genuine breadth comes from the variety of impact dimensions at Nodes 2 and 3.

modes.reason: Evaluating against criteria requires students to make a judgement and back it with evidence — met/partially met/unmet is a three-way assessment that demands more than 'yes' or 'no'. Scaffolding the evaluation structure (criterion → evidence from solution → judgement → implication) prevents students from producing opinion-based assessments dressed as criteria evaluation.

nodes.label: Analysing impact of existing solutions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse the possible future impact of existing digital solutions across economic, environmental and social dimensions to inform their own design.
criteria: Identifies at least one impact across at least one dimension
Explains whether the impact is positive, negative or mixed with reasoning
Identifies a trade-off between dimensions where relevant

width.minimum: Identify at least one possible future impact of an existing solution across one dimension; explain whether the impact is positive, negative or mixed.
width.typical: Analyse a solution across at least two dimensions; identify both positive and negative impacts; explain trade-offs where a solution benefits one dimension but costs another
wider: Research how cloud computing services create sustainability trade-offs — decreased data loss but vast electricity consumption for servers
Investigate how a specific technology (e.g. recommendation algorithms, ride-sharing platforms) has produced unintended social or economic consequences

modes.reason: Analysing impact across different technology types (cloud services, recommendation algorithms, ride-sharing) helps students see that positive and negative impacts co-occur across contexts and dimensions. Single-technology impact analysis risks treating the technology as uniquely harmful or beneficial.

nodes.label: Safety, misinformation and ethical risks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate digital solutions for safety risks, misinformation potential and ethical concerns, and assess whether solutions protect users appropriately
criteria: Identifies at least one safety, misinformation or ethical risk in a solution
Explains who is affected by the risk and how
Suggests at least one design change that would reduce an identified risk

width.minimum: Identify at least one safety or ethical risk in a given digital solution; explain who is affected and how
width.typical: Evaluate a solution for safety risks (user control, privacy defaults), misinformation potential (AI-generated content, recommendation amplification), and ethical concerns; suggest design changes that would reduce identified risks
wider: Evaluate how AI-generated content on social media platforms creates misinformation risks — the potential for high volumes of automatically generated misleading content
Assess a real platform used by students against Safety by Design principles — does it enable users to control their safety and experience?

modes.reason: Safety, misinformation and ethical risks integrate the criteria evaluation (Node 1) and impact analysis (Node 2) into a more demanding evaluative task — students must identify a risk, explain who is affected, and suggest a design change, which requires drawing on both prior nodes simultaneously.

nodes.label: Evaluating your solution against criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can systematically evaluate their own digital solution against design criteria and user stories, identifying where it meets, partially meets or fails to meet requirements.
criteria: Evaluates own solution against specific criteria rather than personal preference
Identifies whether each criterion is met, partially met or unmet
Provides evidence from the solution to support each judgement

width.minimum: Evaluate your own solution against at least two design criteria and one user story; state whether each is met and explain why.
width.typical: Evaluate a solution against multiple criteria and user stories; distinguish between fully met, partially met and unmet requirements; suggest specific improvements for unmet requirements
wider: Evaluate a real commercial platform against Safety by Design principles for young people — are privacy settings comprehensive, easy to use, and set to maximum protection by default?

Limited width — evaluation against criteria is a consistent analytical process. More criteria or more solutions is practice, not broader application. The genuine breadth comes from the variety of impact dimensions at Nodes 2 and 3.

modes.reason: Evaluating against criteria requires students to make a judgement and back it with evidence — met/partially met/unmet is a three-way assessment that demands more than 'yes' or 'no'. Scaffolding the evaluation structure (criterion → evidence from solution → judgement → implication) prevents students from producing opinion-based assessments dressed as criteria evaluation.

nodes.label: Analysing impact of your solution
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse the possible future impact of their own digital solution across economic, environmental and social dimensions.
criteria: Identifies at least one impact across at least one dimension
Explains whether the impact is positive, negative or mixed with reasoning
Identifies a trade-off between dimensions where relevant

width.minimum: Identify at least one possible future impact of your own solution across one dimension; explain whether the impact is positive, negative or mixed.
width.typical: Analyse a solution across at least two dimensions; identify both positive and negative impacts; explain trade-offs where a solution benefits one dimension but costs another
wider: Research how cloud computing services create sustainability trade-offs — decreased data loss but vast electricity consumption for servers
Investigate how a specific technology (e.g. recommendation algorithms, ride-sharing platforms) has produced unintended social or economic consequences

modes.reason: Analysing impact across different technology types (cloud services, recommendation algorithms, ride-sharing) helps students see that positive and negative impacts co-occur across contexts and dimensions. Single-technology impact analysis risks treating the technology as uniquely harmful or beneficial.

descriptors.title: Use digital tools efficiently
descriptors.description: Select and use a range of digital tools efficiently, including unfamiliar features, to create, locate and communicate content, consistently applying common conventions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can select and use appropriate digital tools to create, locate and communicate content, applying common conventions (AC9TDI6P07). They have used familiar tools but have not yet explored unfamiliar features to improve efficiency, used generative AI for content creation, or consistently applied conventions including heading hierarchy, captions and inclusive language.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select and use digital tools efficiently, including exploring unfamiliar features to improve their work; create, locate and communicate content while consistently applying common conventions including heading hierarchy, captions and inclusive language.

nodes.label: Selecting tools for purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select appropriate digital tools for a specific communication task and explain why the chosen tool suits the purpose and audience
criteria: Selects a tool appropriate for the communication task
Explains why the tool suits the purpose or audience

width.minimum: Given a communication task, select an appropriate tool and explain why it suits the task
width.typical: Compare tools for the same task; explain how tool selection affects audience reach, format and accessibility
wider: Investigate how tool selection affects audience reach and accessibility — why a video might reach some audiences better than a document, or why accessibility features matter for inclusive communication

nodes.label: Applying conventions consistently
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply common conventions consistently when creating content, including heading hierarchy, captions, logical storage and inclusive language
criteria: Content uses at least two conventions correctly and consistently
Project files are stored in a logical location with clear naming

width.minimum: Create content that applies at least two conventions (e.g. heading hierarchy and captions); organise project files in a logical storage location
width.typical: Apply conventions consistently across a project including heading hierarchy, captions for images, gender-inclusive language, and logical storage with an outline for collaborators
wider: Limited width — conventions are a fixed set of practices. More conventions applied is completeness, not broader context. The genuine breadth is in the variety of communication tasks they are applied to.

modes.reason: Conventions must be applied consistently across a project — inconsistent application is more harmful than not knowing a convention. What helps is repeated practice across different content types until consistent application is habitual, not exposure to more conventions.

nodes.label: Exploring unfamiliar features and AI tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore unfamiliar features of digital tools to improve efficiency, including using generative AI with effective prompts
criteria: Identifies and uses at least one unfamiliar feature to improve a task
Explains what the feature changed about the quality or efficiency of the work

width.minimum: Identify and use at least one unfamiliar feature of a tool to improve the quality or efficiency of a task; explain what improved
width.typical: Use effective prompts with a generative AI model to create content suited to a specific task (e.g. specifying voice, tone, brevity); use progressive prompting to refine output
wider: Use a progressive series of prompts to refine AI-generated output and evaluate each iteration — what improved, what was lost, and when to stop refining
Compare AI-generated content with manually created content for the same task — evaluate which is more effective and why

modes.reason: Exploring unfamiliar features across different tool types (document editors, AI models, spreadsheets) builds the general capability to learn tools independently. Each tool type requires a different exploration strategy — breadth here is breadth of tool exploration contexts.

descriptors.title: Manage agile projects
descriptors.description: Select and use a range of digital tools efficiently and responsibly to share content online, and plan and manage individual and collaborative agile projects
descriptors.knowledge: Students can select and use appropriate digital tools to share content, plan tasks and collaborate on projects (AC9TDI6P08). They have collaborated using shared tools but have not yet managed projects using agile practices, recorded tasks with responsibilities and timeframes, or applied cultural protocols in collaborative contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select and use digital tools responsibly to share content online, and plan and manage agile projects by setting up shared spaces, recording tasks with responsibilities and timeframes, and demonstrating agile practices across a project.

nodes.label: Planning tasks and timeframes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can record tasks, responsibilities and timeframes for a project using digital tools
criteria: Records at least three tasks with responsibilities and timeframes
Tasks are sequenced in a logical order

width.minimum: Create a task list for a project with at least three tasks, who is responsible for each, and when each is due
width.typical: Use a spreadsheet or project management tool to record tasks with sequence, critical dates and responsibilities; identify which tasks depend on others being completed first
wider: Use AI tools to decompose high-level project instructions into detailed steps; critically evaluate whether the AI's breakdown is complete and correctly sequenced
Limited width — task planning is a process applied the same way regardless of project. The variety comes from the project itself, not the planning method.

nodes.label: Demonstrating agile practices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate agile project management by working in iterative cycles, reviewing progress and adapting plans
criteria: Completes at least one review-and-adapt cycle during the project
Can explain what changed in the plan and why

width.minimum: Complete at least one review-and-adapt cycle during a project — review what has been done, identify what needs to change, update the plan
width.typical: Demonstrate agile practices across a project — regular check-ins, iterative development, adapting plans based on feedback; set up and manage a shared collaborative space
wider: Investigate how agile practices differ across professional contexts — how a software team's sprint differs from a design studio's iterative process
Evaluate how the agile approach changed the project outcome compared to what a linear plan would have produced

nodes.label: Sharing content responsibly
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share content online using digital tools responsibly, demonstrating awareness of appropriate behaviours and cultural sensitivity
criteria: Shares content using an appropriate digital tool
Demonstrates at least one responsible behaviour when sharing

width.minimum: Share content using a digital tool; demonstrate at least one responsible behaviour (e.g. respecting privacy, appropriate attribution)
width.typical: Share content demonstrating empathy for diverse cultural expectations — showing sensitivity around images or names of deceased people, valuing intellectual property and perspectives of others
wider: Apply cultural protocols when collaborating with First Nations community groups on digital projects, including relevant permissions, attributions and acknowledgement of diversity
Limited width — responsible sharing is a consistent set of practices. The breadth comes from the cultural contexts they are applied in.

modes.reason: Responsible sharing in different cultural contexts (general online, First Nations community collaboration) requires students to adapt their behaviour to different norms and protocols. A single context risks treating responsibility as a fixed checklist rather than a context-sensitive practice.

descriptors.title: Multi-factor auth and phishing
descriptors.description: Explain how multi-factor authentication protects an account when the password is compromised and identify phishing and other cyber security threats
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use unique passphrases across accounts and explain the risks of password re-use (AC9TDI6P09). They understand password-based security but have not yet explored what happens when passwords are compromised, how MFA adds a second layer of protection, or how phishing attacks exploit human behaviour.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how multi-factor authentication protects an account even when the password is compromised, and identify phishing and other cyber security threats by recognising the techniques attackers use to exploit users.

nodes.label: When passwords fail
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how a password can be compromised and why password-only security is insufficient
criteria: Names at least two ways a password can be compromised
Explains why password-only security is insufficient
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand how passwords can be compromised cannot reason about why MFA is necessary at Node 2. The attack scenario (password obtained → attacker tries to log in → MFA blocks them) only makes sense if students understand the first step. Without it, MFA appears as arbitrary additional friction rather than a principled response.

width.minimum: Name at least two ways a password can be compromised (e.g. data breach, guessing, shoulder surfing); explain why this means passwords alone are not enough
width.typical: Explain how password reuse amplifies the impact of a single breach; connect to prior knowledge about unique passphrases
wider: Limited width — password compromise is a small set of scenarios. The genuine breadth comes from how MFA and phishing awareness respond to these scenarios at later nodes.

modes.reason: Students who understand only one attack vector (e.g. guessing) do not grasp why password-only security is fundamentally insufficient. Seeing multiple compromise vectors (breach, phishing, shoulder surfing, reuse amplification) establishes that no single password hygiene practice is enough — which is why MFA exists.

nodes.label: How MFA protects accounts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how multi-factor authentication adds a second layer of protection by requiring something beyond the password
criteria: Explains that MFA requires something beyond the password
Explains how MFA protects an account when the password is compromised

width.minimum: Explain that MFA requires a second factor (e.g. SMS code, one-time password) in addition to the password; explain how this protects the account even when the password is compromised
width.typical: Explain how MFA works in practice using a specific example (e.g. bank transfer requiring SMS token); identify different types of second factors (SMS, authenticator app, biometric)
wider: Evaluate how MFA implementation varies across platforms — why some platforms use SMS while others use authenticator apps, and which is more secure
Limited width — MFA is a single concept with a small number of implementations. More platforms is useful comparison but the core understanding is the same.

modes.reason: The protection MFA offers is only clear when students reason through the attack scenario: attacker has password → tries to log in → MFA requires second factor → attacker does not have it → account is protected. Students who accept 'MFA is more secure' without tracing this chain cannot explain why it works or when it would fail.

nodes.label: Identifying phishing and cyber threats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify phishing and other cyber security threats by recognising the techniques used to exploit users
criteria: Identifies at least one phishing technique
Explains how the technique exploits the user (not just that it is dangerous)

width.minimum: Identify at least one phishing technique (e.g. unofficial email domain, urgency language, suspicious links); explain how it tries to exploit the user
width.typical: Identify multiple phishing techniques including email domain spoofing, grammatical errors as filtering mechanisms, and social engineering tactics; explain how each exploits human behaviour rather than technical vulnerabilities
wider: Investigate a real phishing case and analyse the specific techniques used — what made it convincing and what were the red flags?
Research how social engineering exploits human behaviour beyond phishing — pretexting, baiting, tailgating — as cyber security threats that technology alone cannot prevent

modes.reason: Phishing identification requires accumulating a repertoire of attack patterns — students need to recognise multiple techniques (domain spoofing, urgency, suspicious links, grammatical markers) rather than one. A broader repertoire means more robust identification in unfamiliar phishing examples.

descriptors.title: Manage digital footprint data
descriptors.description: Investigate and manage the digital footprint existing systems and student solutions collect and assess if the data is essential to their purpose
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how their digital footprint is created and permanent, and consider privacy when collecting user data (AC9TDI6P10). They understand that a footprint exists but have not yet investigated what specific data systems collect, assessed whether that data is essential, or managed their own footprint settings.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate what digital footprint data existing systems and student solutions collect, manage their own footprint by reviewing privacy settings, and assess whether the data collected is essential to the system's purpose.

nodes.label: What data systems collect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate what digital footprint data a system collects about its users
criteria: Identifies at least three types of data a platform collects
Includes at least one type of data collected passively (not explicitly provided by the user)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot name what categories of data a system collects cannot assess whether that data is essential (Node 2) or make informed decisions about privacy settings (Node 3). The investigation at Node 1 is the factual foundation for both subsequent analytical tasks.

width.minimum: Given a platform or app, identify at least three types of data it collects about users (e.g. location, browsing history, contacts, usage patterns)
width.typical: Research a platform's privacy policy to identify what data is collected, how it is used, and how long it is stored; compare data collection across two platforms
wider: Investigate how recommendation algorithms used in music or video streaming services rely on tracking user habits to generate personalised content
Research how data collection practices differ between platforms marketed to young people vs adults

modes.reason: Investigating data collection across different platform types (social media, streaming services, youth-targeted apps) reveals that collection practices vary systematically with business model and audience. Multiple platform contexts help students see the pattern rather than treating a single platform as representative.

nodes.label: Assessing whether data is essential
nodes.checkpoint: Students can assess whether the data a system collects is essential to its purpose, or whether it exceeds what is needed
criteria: Identifies at least one essential and one non-essential data item for a given system
Explains why each is or is not essential to the system's purpose

width.minimum: Given a system and the data it collects, identify at least one piece of data that is essential to its purpose and one that is not; explain the difference
width.typical: Assess the appropriateness of data collected by surveys or platforms — for example, identifying that providing your address is not necessary for a food preferences survey but is appropriate for a Census
wider: Evaluate whether the data collected by a student-built solution is essential — apply the same critical lens to their own design decisions
Research how the Australian Privacy Principles define data minimisation and apply this standard to a real platform

modes.reason: Assessing whether data is essential requires students to reason from purpose: what does this system do? → what data does it need to do that? → is this collected item necessary for that purpose? Students who cannot articulate the system's purpose cannot make the essential/non-essential distinction — they need the reasoning chain, not just the binary label.

nodes.label: Managing your digital footprint
nodes.checkpoint: Students can review and manage their own digital footprint by adjusting privacy settings and making informed decisions about data sharing
criteria: Reviews privacy settings on at least one platform
Identifies at least one setting to change and explains the reasoning

width.minimum: Review privacy settings on at least one platform they use; identify at least one setting they would change and explain why
width.typical: Review and manage privacy settings across multiple platforms; set defaults to maximum protection; explain the trade-off between functionality and privacy for specific settings
wider: Evaluate the risks of sharing personal data given that generative AI can create deepfake content from short videos and audio recordings
Investigate how privacy settings interact with recommendation systems — what changes in the user experience when data collection is restricted?

modes.reason: Managing footprint settings across different platforms (social media, streaming, gaming) requires students to apply the same essential/non-essential judgement in different contexts where defaults and trade-offs differ. Breadth here is breadth of platform contexts and privacy trade-off types.

descriptors.title: Acquire, store and validate data
descriptors.description: develop techniques to acquire, store and validate data from a range of sources using software, including spreadsheets and databases
descriptors.knowledge: Students can acquire, store and validate data from a range of sources using spreadsheets and databases (AC9TDI8P01). They can identify data quality issues including relevance, correctness, currency and potential bias. They have not yet developed automated validation techniques, applied the Australian Privacy Principles to data collection, or considered training data issues for predictive models.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop techniques — including automated validation, privacy-compliant acquisition, and bias-aware evaluation — to acquire, store and validate data from a range of sources using spreadsheets and databases.

nodes.label: Designing systems that collect structured data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design and develop a system that collects structured data from users, with appropriate fields and data types.
criteria: Data collection system captures at least two distinct data types
Collected data is stored in a structured format accessible for analysis
nodes.hinge_reason: Poorly designed data collection structure cascades through N2, N3 and N4 — automated validation cannot be built on an undefined schema, privacy compliance cannot be assessed without knowing what data is collected, and source comparison is meaningless without a clear collection target.

width.minimum: Design and build a data collection form or interface that captures at least two data types (e.g. numeric rating and text comment); store collected data in a structured format.
width.typical: Design a data collection system for a specific purpose (e.g. a review or feedback system); define appropriate field types, required fields, and storage format; explain how the structure supports later analysis.
wider: Design a data collection system for a community need (e.g. event feedback, local environment monitoring) and consider what structural decisions support the community's analytical needs
Compare how different Likert scale configurations (3-point vs 5-point vs 7-point) affect the quality of data collected and what statistical operations become possible

modes.reason: Data collection system design requires students to reason from the analytical question backward to field types and schema — students who jump to implementation without this reasoning produce ad-hoc schemas that cannot be validated or analysed. The scaffold: question → required data → field types → storage structure.

nodes.label: Automated validation techniques
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop automated validation techniques that check data is correct and meaningful using both rules and UI constraints.
criteria: Implements at least one automated validation rule that prevents an identifiable class of bad data
Explains what the rule catches and at least one case it would not catch
nodes.hinge_reason: Unvalidated data renders downstream analysis unreliable — students who cannot implement validation collect data they cannot trust, and any privacy compliance decisions or source comparisons built on bad data produce meaningless conclusions.

width.minimum: Implement at least one automated validation rule (e.g. input range constraint, data type check, or required field check) and explain what it prevents.
width.typical: Implement multiple validation techniques — UI element constraints, rule-based checks, and at least one statistical technique (e.g. detecting outliers or inconsistent ratings); explain what each technique catches and what it cannot catch.
wider: Implement validation that detects potential bias in collected responses (e.g. all 5-star reviews from a single IP address) and explain the statistical reasoning
Investigate how automated content moderation systems combine rule-based and ML-based validation — what each approach handles well and where each fails
Consider training data issues such as the zero problem — what happens when a predictive model has no training examples for a valid input category, and how validation can surface this

modes.reason: Validation design requires students to reason from the threat (what could go wrong?) to the check (how would we detect it?) to the implementation. Without this reasoning scaffold, students implement surface-level checks without thinking about what attack or error each check addresses.

nodes.label: Privacy-compliant data acquisition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can acquire and store data in accordance with the Australian Privacy Principles, protecting personally identifiable information from unauthorised access.
criteria: Identifies at least one personally identifiable data element in a system
Explains at least one APP requirement that applies to that data and how the system satisfies or violates it

width.minimum: Identify at least one personally identifiable element in a data collection system and explain what the Australian Privacy Principles require for that data.
width.typical: Design a data collection system that acquires data according to the Australian Privacy Principles — limiting collection to what is necessary, protecting PII from public exposure, and ensuring data is not shared without consent; explain the specific APP requirements applied.
wider: Evaluate an existing data collection system (e.g. a school app, community platform) against the Australian Privacy Principles — identify gaps and recommend improvements
Investigate how systems collecting data from or about First Nations Australians must also address Indigenous data sovereignty principles, and how these extend beyond the APPs
Compare how data protection requirements differ across jurisdictions (APPs in Australia, GDPR in Europe) and explain the implications for systems used globally

modes.reason: Privacy compliance is abstract without concrete cases. Students need to apply APP requirements to different data types — health data, location data, contact data — to understand how the principles operate in practice rather than as a compliance checklist.

nodes.label: Comparing and selecting data sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the strengths and weaknesses of different data collection methods and select sources appropriate to a given investigation.
criteria: Identifies at least two data collection methods and a specific strength and weakness of each
Justifies selection of a method for a specific investigation with reference to its strengths relative to the question

width.minimum: Given a research question, identify two different data collection methods and describe one strength and one weakness of each.
width.typical: Compare at least three data collection methods (e.g. online survey, observation, existing dataset such as ABS); explain how each method's strengths and weaknesses affect its suitability for a specific question; select the most appropriate method and justify.
wider: Access and store ABS population data in a format suitable for analysis; evaluate what questions the dataset can and cannot answer
Investigate how browser history, phone logs or social media data are collected passively — compare this to consent-based collection and evaluate the ethical difference
Design a mixed-method data collection approach that compensates for the weaknesses of each individual method

modes.reason: Students default to surveys. Broader exposure to source types — existing datasets, observation, passive collection, interviews — builds a more complete picture of the data acquisition landscape and what each method is and isn't suited for.

descriptors.title: Analyse and visualise data
descriptors.description: analyse and visualise data interactively using a range of software, including spreadsheets and databases, to draw conclusions and make predictions by identifying trends and outliers
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse and visualise data using a range of software including spreadsheets and databases (AC9TDI8P02). They can identify trends and patterns in data and draw conclusions from visualisations. They have not yet developed interactive visualisations, applied machine learning as a form of analysis, or adjusted model parameters to observe effects on predictions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and visualise data interactively using spreadsheets and databases to draw conclusions and make predictions by identifying trends and outliers, including developing interactive visualisations and exploring how machine learning models analyse patterns in data.

nodes.label: Summarising data and identifying trends
nodes.checkpoint: Students can summarise a dataset by identifying its attributes, relationships between variables, trends and outliers.
criteria: Identifies at least one trend in a dataset and describes its direction
Identifies at least one outlier and explains whether it represents an error or a genuine data point
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify trends and outliers in a dataset cannot draw conclusions or make predictions at N2 — the N2 checkpoint is directly dependent on the data summary produced at N1.

width.minimum: Given a dataset, identify at least one trend and one outlier; describe what each indicates about the data.
width.typical: Summarise a dataset's attributes and the relationships between variables; identify multiple trends and outliers; explain what each finding suggests and whether outliers are errors or genuinely interesting data points.
wider: Summarise electoral data including demographics, historical swings and exceptions — identify what trends predict outcomes and where exceptions undermine simple predictions
Investigate why the same dataset can show different trends depending on how it is grouped or filtered — connecting this to statistical concepts of aggregation

modes.reason: Trend and outlier identification requires systematic data reading — students who scan data intuitively often miss outliers or misread trend direction. Scaffolding the analysis (describe the range → identify central tendency → find exceptions → name the direction) produces reliable summary before prediction.

nodes.label: Drawing conclusions and making predictions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw conclusions from data analysis and make predictions, including identifying the limits of the prediction.
criteria: States a conclusion that is grounded in the data (not just restating the data)
Makes a prediction and identifies at least one assumption or limitation
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify limiting assumptions for predictions cannot meaningfully design interactive visualisations at N3 — the analytical intent of the visualisation depends on knowing what question is being asked and what its limitations are.

width.minimum: Draw at least one conclusion from a dataset and make one prediction; note one limitation of the prediction.
width.typical: Draw multiple conclusions from a dataset with different variables; make predictions by extending observed trends; identify what would need to be true for the predictions to hold and where they might fail.
wider: Investigate emerging trends in Australia's industries using ABS data — make predictions about future employment patterns and identify what assumptions underpin each prediction
Analyse historical data to predict a future outcome (election, environmental trend, economic indicator) and explain what factors could cause the prediction to be wrong

modes.reason: Students often confuse correlation with causation when making predictions, or state predictions without identifying their limiting assumptions. A reasoning scaffold — what does the trend show? → what would have to be true for this to continue? → what could break this pattern? — builds rigour in prediction-making.

nodes.label: Developing interactive visualisations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop interactive visualisations for exploring complex data, allowing users to control and view different aspects of a dataset.
criteria: Visualisation includes at least one interactive element that changes what is displayed
The interaction serves an analytical purpose — it helps the user explore the data, not just decorative

width.minimum: Create a visualisation with at least one interactive element (e.g. a filter, slider, or chart type selector) that allows a user to change what is displayed.
width.typical: Develop an interactive visualisation for a complex dataset — include multiple views or filters that allow exploration of relationships, trends and outliers; explain how the interactive design helps users explore the data.
wider: Develop a motion chart or time-series interactive visualisation (e.g. population, life expectancy and fertility rate) that allows users to explore change over time
Design an interactive dashboard with linked views where selecting a data point in one chart filters or highlights related data in another
Incorporate sliders to allow users to adjust visualisation parameters and observe the effect on how patterns appear

modes.reason: Interactive visualisation requires coordinating data analysis, visual design and interactivity implementation. Students who understand each individually often struggle to build a visualisation that is both analytically useful and usable. The integration node is where analysis intent, visual form and interaction mechanism must work together.

nodes.label: Machine learning as a form of data analysis
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how machine learning trains algorithms on data to identify patterns and classify inputs, and explore how adjusting model parameters affects outputs.
criteria: Correctly explains that ML algorithms learn patterns from training data
Demonstrates that changing training data or parameters changes model output
Can explain in plain language what changed and why

width.minimum: Describe what machine learning is and explain, using one example, how an algorithm is trained on data to classify new inputs.
width.typical: Use a machine learning tool to train a model on a dataset and classify new inputs; adjust at least one parameter and observe how it changes the model's output; explain what the parameter controls.
wider: Explore how adjusting the weighting of different input variables in a model changes its predictions — explain what this reveals about which variables have most influence
Investigate how training data composition affects model output — what happens when certain categories are underrepresented? Connect this to real-world bias in deployed AI systems
Use a visual ML tool (e.g. Teachable Machine) to train image classifiers and observe how classification accuracy changes as training data volume increases

modes.reason: Machine learning is conceptually opaque — students often treat it as a black box. Multiple hands-on experiments (image classification, parameter adjustment, training data variation) each make a different aspect of the process visible, building a more complete mental model than a single experiment.

descriptors.title: Model and query entities and relationships
descriptors.description: model and query entities and their relationships using structured data
descriptors.knowledge: Students can model and query the attributes of objects and events using structured data (AC9TDI8P03). They have experience with single-table databases and basic queries. They have not yet modelled multi-entity relationships, created relational data schemas, or written SQL queries with JOIN operations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students model entities and their relationships using a relational data schema, build a structured database, and query it using SQL including SELECT, WHERE and simple JOIN/GROUP BY clauses.

nodes.label: Modelling entities and their attributes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify entities, their attributes, and the relationships between them for a given domain.
criteria: Identifies at least two distinct entities with their respective attributes
Correctly identifies at least one relationship between entities (including its type — one-to-many or many-to-many)
nodes.hinge_reason: Entity and relationship modelling errors cascade directly into N2 schema design — a student who misidentifies entities or omits a relationship cannot design a correct schema, and all downstream database build and query work inherits the error.

width.minimum: Identify at least two entities in a given scenario, list their attributes, and describe one relationship between them.
width.typical: Model a multi-entity domain (e.g. movies, users and reviews) by identifying all entities, their attributes, and the relationships between them; represent the model as an entity-relationship diagram or equivalent.
wider: Model a community data scenario (e.g. a local First Nations language archive with speakers, words and recordings) — identify entities, attributes and relationships specific to the community's needs
Compare how the same domain can be modelled differently depending on the questions the database needs to answer — explain the implications of each modelling choice

modes.reason: Entity modelling requires systematic domain reasoning — what things exist? what are their properties? how do they relate? Students who approach this intuitively often omit entities or model relationships as attributes. Scaffolding the domain analysis step by step prevents schema design from inheriting modelling errors.

nodes.label: Designing a relational database schema
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design a relational database schema with multiple tables, primary keys and foreign keys that captures the entities and relationships in their model.
criteria: Schema has at least two tables each with a primary key
A foreign key correctly links the tables and reflects the modelled relationship
Data types are appropriate for each attribute
nodes.hinge_reason: Schema design errors (wrong primary/foreign keys, wrong data types, missing relationships) propagate directly into N3 — a student cannot build a correct database from an incorrect schema, and subsequent queries will fail or return wrong results.

width.minimum: Design at least two database tables with a primary key in each and a foreign key linking them; explain what the foreign key relationship represents.
width.typical: Design a relational schema for a multi-entity domain; define primary keys, foreign keys and appropriate data types for each attribute; explain how the schema enforces the relationships between entities.
wider: Design a schema that resolves a many-to-many relationship using a junction table — explain why this is necessary and how the junction table works
Evaluate an existing schema for redundancy and normalisation issues — identify what problems the original design causes and how to resolve them

modes.reason: Schema design requires students to reason from the entity model to implementation decisions: which entity owns the foreign key? What data type suits each attribute? How do we represent a many-to-many relationship? Without a reasoning scaffold, students produce schemas by intuition and make structural errors that are hard to debug.

nodes.label: Building and populating the database
nodes.checkpoint: Students can build a database from a schema and populate it with data that reflects real-world entities and their relationships.
criteria: Database tables exist and are populated with data
Relationships between tables are represented correctly in the data (foreign key values match parent primary keys)
nodes.hinge_reason: A database that is incorrectly built or incompletely populated cannot be queried at N4 — SQL errors at N3 (missing tables, foreign key violations, wrong data types) prevent any query from executing correctly.

width.minimum: Build at least two linked tables from a schema; insert enough data to test the relationships (at least one parent and two child records).
width.typical: Build a database from a designed schema; populate it with sufficient data to support the queries needed to solve the problem; ensure that foreign key constraints are satisfied in the inserted data.
wider: Populate a database using data imported from an existing source (CSV or spreadsheet) rather than manually — explain any transformation required to fit the schema
Deliberately insert data that violates foreign key constraints and observe how the database enforces referential integrity — explain what this prevents

modes.reason: SQL data definition and insertion requires syntactic precision. Students need sufficient practice with CREATE TABLE, INSERT INTO, and constraint specification before they can fluently build databases from schemas. Errors at this stage cascade into query failures that are harder to debug.

nodes.label: Querying with SELECT, WHERE and JOIN
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write SQL queries using SELECT, WHERE and JOIN to retrieve and filter data across multiple tables.
criteria: Correctly writes a SELECT/WHERE query that filters data by a specified condition
Correctly writes a JOIN query that combines data from two tables
Output matches what the question asks for

width.minimum: Write at least one SQL query that uses SELECT and WHERE to filter rows from a single table, and one query that uses JOIN to combine data from two tables.
width.typical: Write queries using SELECT, WHERE, JOIN and GROUP BY/COUNT to retrieve, filter, aggregate and count data across multiple tables; explain what each clause does and why it is needed for the given question.
wider: Write SQL queries to detect data integrity issues (e.g. confirming each user has only reviewed each movie once using GROUP BY and HAVING COUNT)
Use SQL to answer a real decision-support question (e.g. identifying which products have no reviews, or which users have the highest activity) and explain how the query logic maps to the question
Explore edge cases in JOIN behaviour — what happens with left joins when no match exists, and why this matters for certain queries

modes.reason: SQL queries are best learned through varied question types — each question type (filtering, aggregating, joining, detecting duplicates) requires a different clause combination. Students who only practise SELECT/WHERE often struggle when JOIN logic is needed, or don't know when GROUP BY is appropriate.

descriptors.title: Define and decompose real-world problems
descriptors.description: define and decompose real-world problems with design criteria and by interviewing stakeholders to create user stories
descriptors.knowledge: Students can define and decompose real-world problems with design criteria and by considering the needs of users (AC9TDI8P04). They can identify constraints and requirements. They have not yet conducted stakeholder interviews, formulated user stories from primary research, or defined problems with explicit scope awareness.
descriptors.endpoint: Students define and decompose real-world problems by interviewing stakeholders to create user stories, establishing design criteria with precision and scope awareness.

nodes.label: Eliciting stakeholder needs through interviews
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design and conduct an interview with a stakeholder to elicit their needs, capturing information relevant to defining the problem.
criteria: Conducts an interview using prepared questions
Records the stakeholder's expressed needs accurately
Identifies at least one insight that came from the interview rather than assumption
nodes.hinge_reason: Inadequate stakeholder interviews cascade through the entire design process — user stories at N2 built on unelicited or assumed needs, and a problem definition at N3 that doesn't reflect real stakeholder requirements, produce design criteria at N4 that cannot evaluate whether the right problem is being solved.

width.minimum: Conduct at least one stakeholder interview using prepared questions; record the key needs and perspectives the interviewee expressed.
width.typical: Design interview questions that elicit both specific needs and open-ended responses; conduct the interview; synthesise findings to identify the core stakeholder needs and distinguish explicit requests from underlying goals.
wider: Conduct interviews with stakeholders who have different or conflicting needs — synthesise findings to identify where requirements agree and where they must be reconciled

Explore how interviewing First Nations Australian community members to develop digital solutions requires additional considerations: cultural protocols, community consent, and understanding community-defined needs rather than imposing external problem frames
Compare interview-elicited user needs with assumptions made without interviews — reflect on what would have been designed wrongly without the primary research

modes.reason: Stakeholder interview quality varies enormously with question design. Students who only interview one type of stakeholder (e.g. a peer) often miss how different perspectives create different requirements. Interviewing stakeholders with different roles or needs reveals the problem space more fully.

nodes.label: Creating user stories
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create user stories from stakeholder interview data using the standard template format.
criteria: User stories follow the template format correctly
User stories are grounded in interview data, not assumed needs
Each user story identifies a specific user type, goal and rationale
nodes.hinge_reason: User stories that don't follow the template or aren't grounded in interview data cannot drive problem definition at N3 or design criteria at N4 — the criteria become disconnected from actual stakeholder needs.

width.minimum: Create at least two user stories from interview data using the template: 'As a [user], I want [goal] so that [reason]'.
width.typical: Create a set of user stories from interview findings that cover the key needs identified; ensure each story identifies the user type, goal and rationale; use the stories to drive subsequent design decisions.
wider: Prioritise user stories using a technique such as MoSCoW (must have, should have, could have, won't have) and explain the prioritisation reasoning
Identify ambiguous or conflicting user stories and resolve them through follow-up with stakeholders

modes.reason: User story template compliance requires precision — students commonly omit the 'so that' rationale or write stories from their own perspective rather than the stakeholder's. Sufficient practice with varied stakeholder data builds the habit of template-grounded story creation.

nodes.label: Defining the problem with precision and scope
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write a precise problem definition that names the problem, identifies scope boundaries, and acknowledges what is and isn't solvable within the project.
criteria: Problem definition names the specific problem (not just a domain)
Identifies at least one scope boundary (what is out of scope)
Problem definition is connected to the user stories rather than developed independently
nodes.hinge_reason: A problem definition without scope boundaries makes N4 criteria impossible to evaluate — students cannot check whether criteria are met if the problem itself is not precisely defined.

width.minimum: Write a problem definition statement that names the problem clearly and identifies at least one scope constraint (what is and isn't being solved).
width.typical: Write a problem definition with precision about what the problem is, what it is not, and whether it is solvable in the available timeframe; connect the definition to the user stories; identify questions that need answering before design can begin.
wider: Explore how a broadly framed problem ('How do we encourage people to balance energy intake?') can be decomposed into sub-problems — identify which sub-problems are solvable with a digital system and which are not
Examine how recognising diverse stakeholder perspectives changes the problem definition — what looks like one problem from one stakeholder's view is a different problem from another's

modes.reason: Students tend to leap from a problem statement to a solution before the problem is well-defined. A reasoning scaffold — what exactly is the problem? → for whom? → what would count as solving it? → what is out of scope? — prevents premature solution framing and produces more useful design criteria.

nodes.label: Establishing design criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can establish design criteria derived from user stories and problem definition that will guide evaluation of solutions.
criteria: At least two design criteria are written that are checkable against a solution
Criteria are derived from user stories, not generated independently

width.minimum: Write at least two design criteria derived from user stories; criteria must be assessable (checkable against a solution).
width.typical: Establish a set of design criteria from user stories and problem definition; ensure criteria are specific and assessable; include both functional criteria (what the system does) and non-functional criteria (how it performs or what constraints apply).
wider: Develop design criteria that explicitly account for diverse user needs — including accessibility criteria for users with different abilities
Compare functional and non-functional design criteria for a system and explain why non-functional criteria (e.g. performance, privacy, accessibility) are as important as functional ones

descriptors.title: Design algorithms with logical operators
descriptors.description: design algorithms involving logical operators and represent them as flowcharts and pseudocode
descriptors.knowledge: Students can design algorithms involving nested control structures and represent them as flowcharts and pseudocode (AC9TDI8P05). They have experience with sequence, selection and iteration. They have not yet used Boolean logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) to express compound conditions in control structures.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design algorithms using Boolean logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) to express compound conditions, and represent them as flowcharts and pseudocode.

nodes.label: Boolean logical operators
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the behaviour of AND, OR and NOT and evaluate compound Boolean expressions.
criteria: Correctly evaluates a compound expression with at least two operators
Correctly identifies when an AND expression is false (either operand false) vs when an OR expression is false (both operands false)
nodes.hinge_reason: Boolean operator errors (confusing AND with OR, misapplying NOT) propagate directly into N2 — students who cannot reliably evaluate compound expressions cannot write correct IF conditions, making algorithmic design at N4 unreachable.

width.minimum: Evaluate the truth value of at least three compound Boolean expressions involving AND, OR and NOT; explain what each operator does.
width.typical: Evaluate compound Boolean expressions for multiple input combinations; describe in plain language what condition each compound expression represents; identify when a condition will be true and when false for AND, OR and NOT combinations.
wider: Use truth tables to systematically evaluate all combinations for two-variable AND, OR and NOT expressions
Translate a plain-language rule (e.g. 'a person can vote if they are 18 or older AND are a registered citizen') into a Boolean expression and verify it

modes.reason: Boolean operator evaluation requires precision — students commonly confuse AND (both must be true) with OR (at least one must be true), and misapply NOT. Sufficient practice with varied expressions, including edge cases, builds reliable operator intuition before algorithm design.

nodes.label: Using logical operators in control structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use Boolean operations in IF conditions to express compound requirements in algorithms.
criteria: IF condition using at least one logical operator correctly captures the stated compound requirement
Algorithm produces correct output when traced with at least two different inputs
nodes.hinge_reason: An incorrect compound condition in an IF statement makes N3 representation invalid — students represent and communicate an algorithm that does not solve the problem, and N4 design is built on faulty logic.

width.minimum: Write or interpret an IF condition using AND, OR or NOT that correctly captures a compound requirement; trace through the algorithm with at least two inputs.
width.typical: Design IF conditions using combinations of AND, OR and NOT to express compound conditions; trace the algorithm with multiple inputs including boundary cases; explain why the compound condition correctly captures the intended logic.
wider: Design an algorithm that uses nested logical operators — a condition within a condition — and explain the evaluation order
Analyse an algorithm with a logical operator error and explain what incorrect behaviour it causes and how to fix it

modes.reason: Writing correct compound conditions requires students to reason from the intent (what should happen and when?) to the expression (how do I write that as a Boolean condition?). Without this direction, students write conditions by trial and error, producing subtle logic errors that are hard to detect.

nodes.label: Representing algorithms as flowcharts and pseudocode
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent algorithms that use logical operators as both flowcharts and pseudocode, using precise and unambiguous notation.
criteria: Flowchart or pseudocode correctly represents the algorithm's logic including at least one compound Boolean condition
Notation is unambiguous — another person could implement the algorithm from the representation

width.minimum: Represent one algorithm with a compound Boolean condition as either a flowchart OR pseudocode with correct notation.
width.typical: Represent the same algorithm using both flowchart and pseudocode; use precise pseudocode notation (e.g. IF [condition] AND [condition] THEN); explain how the two representations describe the same algorithm.
wider: Represent a complex algorithm — involving multiple compound conditions and nested structures — as both a flowchart and pseudocode; explain how readability differs between the two forms and when each is more useful
Translate between a decision tree (e.g. animal classification) and pseudocode — identify the equivalent control structures in each representation

nodes.label: Designing algorithms for real problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design algorithms involving logical operators to solve a specified real-world problem, including modifying existing algorithms.
criteria: Algorithm correctly handles the primary case
Algorithm handles at least one edge case (e.g. boundary input, conflicting conditions)
Algorithm can be traced to verify correct output
