width.minimum: Design an algorithm with at least one compound Boolean condition that correctly solves a specified problem, OR modify an existing algorithm to fix or extend it.
width.typical: Design or modify an algorithm that uses AND, OR and NOT to solve a problem with multiple conditions — represent it as both flowchart and pseudocode, and verify it handles edge cases correctly.
wider: Design an algorithm to detect whether two shapes intersect, including the edge case where shapes just touch — represent and verify with test cases
Design an algorithm with Boolean conditions for a decision-making context (e.g. eligibility checking, sensor-triggered automation) and evaluate it against a range of scenarios
Extend an existing algorithm with new requirements expressed as additional Boolean conditions — explain how the extension changes the algorithm's behaviour

modes.reason: Nodes 1–3 address Boolean operators, compound conditions and representation separately. The design node requires students to coordinate all three — understanding what condition is needed, expressing it correctly with Boolean operators, and representing it unambiguously. Students who can do each part individually often struggle to design from scratch.

descriptors.title: Validate algorithms and programs
descriptors.description: validate algorithms and programs by comparing their output against a range of test cases
descriptors.knowledge: Students can trace algorithms to predict output for a given input and identify errors (AC9TDI8P06). They can identify when a program's state is unexpected. They have not yet designed systematic test suites including boundary and invalid input cases, or applied a validation methodology beyond ad-hoc tracing.
descriptors.endpoint: Students validate algorithms and programs by designing and applying a range of test cases — including boundary cases and invalid inputs — to confirm correct behaviour or identify errors.

nodes.label: Tracing algorithms and identifying unexpected state
nodes.checkpoint: Students can trace an algorithm to identify when its state becomes unexpected, why this occurred, and what change is needed.
criteria: Records the state of key variables at each step of the algorithm
Identifies the step where state becomes unexpected and explains why
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot systematically trace algorithm state cannot identify boundary conditions at N2 — boundary test design requires knowing what the algorithm does at each step to determine where its behaviour changes.

width.minimum: Trace an algorithm step by step, record the state of each variable at each step, and identify one point where the state is unexpected.
width.typical: Trace an algorithm with a bug; identify the exact step where the state diverges from expected; explain why the bug occurred (e.g. off-by-one, wrong condition, incorrect variable) and describe the fix needed.
wider: Trace an algorithm involving nested loops or nested conditions, tracking the state of multiple variables simultaneously
Compare two algorithms that produce the same output for most inputs but differ at an edge case — explain what the difference is and which is correct

modes.reason: Algorithm tracing requires precision and discipline. Students who skip steps or guess at state values often fail to locate bugs correctly. Sufficient practice with varied algorithms — including those with intentional bugs — builds the systematic tracing habit.

nodes.label: Designing boundary test cases
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify boundary conditions for an algorithm or program and design test cases that verify boundary behaviour is handled correctly.
criteria: Identifies at least one genuine boundary condition (not just a typical input)
Designs a test case that specifically targets the boundary
Explains what correct behaviour at the boundary should be
nodes.hinge_reason: A test suite without boundary cases at N4 does not constitute systematic validation — the descriptor specifically requires a range of test cases, and boundary cases are the most likely failure points in algorithmic implementations.

width.minimum: For a given algorithm, identify at least one boundary condition and write a test case that checks it; explain what the test case is checking.
width.typical: Identify the full set of boundary conditions for an algorithm (e.g. minimum/maximum valid input, exact equality cases, first/last element of a collection); write test cases for each and explain what each checks.
wider: Determine boundary test cases for a geometric algorithm (e.g. shape intersection when shapes just touch vs overlap vs are separate) and verify each case
Explain why boundary conditions are the most likely place for algorithms to fail and connect this to how conditions are evaluated in code

modes.reason: Identifying boundaries requires systematic reasoning: what values represent the edge of the valid range? What happens at exactly the boundary value vs one above/below? Students who approach testing intuitively often miss the most important boundary case. A structured approach (identify range → find boundary → test at boundary, just inside, just outside) is the key skill.

nodes.label: Testing with invalid inputs and error handling
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generate invalid inputs and user errors and verify that programs handle them appropriately without crashing.
criteria: Tests at least one invalid input type
Identifies whether the program's response to invalid input is appropriate (handled gracefully) or a failure (crashes, silent corruption, wrong output)

width.minimum: Identify at least one type of invalid input for a program; test the program with that input and describe what happened; explain what the correct behaviour should be.
width.typical: Identify multiple categories of invalid input (wrong type, out of range, missing input, unexpected format); test the program against each; verify that errors are handled appropriately rather than causing crashes or silent failures.
wider: Design a systematic set of invalid input tests that covers all categories of potential user error for a specific program
Investigate how professional software uses try/catch or error-handling mechanisms to manage invalid input — compare this to defensive validation at input time

nodes.label: Systematic validation against a test suite
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design and apply a complete test suite that validates an algorithm or program against normal inputs, boundary cases and invalid inputs.
criteria: Test suite includes at least one normal, one boundary and one invalid input test case
Expected output is defined for each test case before testing
Outcome (pass/fail) is recorded for each test case

width.minimum: Design a test suite with at least three test cases (normal, boundary, invalid); apply each to the algorithm or program and record the outcome.
width.typical: Design a complete test suite; apply each test case; record expected vs actual output; for any failed test, trace the algorithm to locate the error and fix it; re-run the test suite to confirm the fix.
wider: Apply the test-fix-retest cycle to a program with multiple bugs, tracking which bugs are introduced or unintentionally fixed by each change
Compare manual test suites with automated testing approaches — explain what automation enables that manual testing cannot scale to
Design a test suite for an algorithm at a peer's solution and explain each test case's purpose to the peer

modes.reason: A complete test suite integrates tracing (node 1), boundary identification (node 2) and invalid input testing (node 3) into a coordinated validation approach. Students who can do each step individually often produce incomplete test suites by defaulting to only normal-case tests. Integration here is recognising what categories of testing are needed and deliberately including all three.

descriptors.title: Design and prototype user experience
descriptors.description: design and prototype the user experience of a digital system
descriptors.knowledge: Students can design the user experience of a digital system, including interface mock-ups and considering user needs (AC9TDI8P07). They have experience with digital design tools. They have not yet prototyped an interactive user experience with clickable flows, or considered all dimensions of UX including emotional, cultural and onboarding experiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design and prototype the user experience of a digital system, including interactive prototypes with clickable flows and consideration of aesthetics, functionality, accessibility, and emotional or cultural user responses.

nodes.label: UX as more than interface — all dimensions of user experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe what user experience means across its full scope — aesthetics, functionality, onboarding, emotional and cultural responses.
criteria: Identifies at least two UX dimensions beyond visual layout
Describes how each dimension affects a user's experience of a specific system
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who reduce UX to visual design cannot complete N2 or N3 — designing for aesthetics + functionality + enjoyment simultaneously, and prototyping a full UX, require the broader conception of UX established at N1.

width.minimum: Describe at least two distinct dimensions of user experience beyond visual layout (e.g. onboarding experience, emotional response, cultural response, task completion feeling).
width.typical: Describe the full scope of user experience for a given digital system — including first-use experience, aesthetic and functional response, and emotional or cultural dimensions; explain how each dimension affects users differently.
wider: Evaluate the first-use onboarding experience of an existing digital system — describe what assumptions it makes about users and where those assumptions fail
Examine how users from different cultural backgrounds experience the same digital system differently — identify design choices that create exclusion and what changes would improve inclusivity

modes.reason: Students typically think of UX as visual design. Multiple contrasting UX dimensions — onboarding, emotional response, cultural response — expand this to the full scope of the descriptor and are better learned through comparison of distinct contexts than through a definition.

nodes.label: Designing for aesthetics, functionality and enjoyment
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design a user experience that integrates aesthetic, functional and enjoyment considerations into a coherent interface.
criteria: Design addresses at least one functional requirement and at least one aesthetic consideration
Student can explain the intention behind specific design choices
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a coherent design intent from N2, the N3 prototype has no basis for its interaction and flow decisions — students prototype arbitrary features rather than a designed experience.

width.minimum: Design an interface that addresses both a functional requirement (what the system does) and an aesthetic choice (how it looks and feels); explain the intention behind each choice.
width.typical: Design a user experience that integrates aesthetics, functionality and the feeling of enjoyment — explain how the design choices work together to create a satisfying user experience; identify trade-offs made between competing design goals.
wider: Design documentation, branding and onboarding materials that extend the UX beyond the screen interactions — explain how consistent branding creates a coherent user experience
Analyse the UX of an existing digital system's getting-started experience — identify what creates a sense of ease or frustration and connect to specific design choices

modes.reason: UX design requires students to reason from intent (what experience?) to choices (which aesthetic and functional decisions serve that intent?) — without this reasoning, design choices are arbitrary. Scaffolding the design decision chain prevents the N3 prototype from being a collection of features rather than a designed experience.

nodes.label: Building an interactive prototype
nodes.checkpoint: Students can prototype a user experience with interactive elements that simulate clickable flows between screens or views.
criteria: Prototype has at least two screens linked by a clickable interaction
A user can complete at least one task using the prototype without narration from the designer

width.minimum: Create a prototype with at least two screens/views linked by a clickable interaction; demonstrate the flow to a peer.
width.typical: Build a prototype of a simple digital system (e.g. mobile app) using a presentation tool or no-code prototyping tool; include multiple screens with clickable interactions that simulate the user's task completion flow; demonstrate the prototype with a test user and identify one improvement.
wider: Create a high-fidelity prototype that includes edge states — empty states, error states, and success confirmations — not just the happy path
Conduct a structured usability test with a prototype — define tasks, observe users completing them, note where they struggle, and use findings to revise the design

modes.reason: A prototype integrates UX understanding (node 1), design intent (node 2) and technical prototype-building skills. Students who understand UX principles often struggle to translate them into an interactive artefact where all the flows must work coherently. The integration challenge is connecting design intent to every specific screen and interaction.

descriptors.title: Generate, modify and critically evaluate alternative designs
descriptors.description: generate, modify, communicate and critically evaluate alternative designs
descriptors.knowledge: Students can generate, modify, communicate and evaluate alternative designs (AC9TDI8P08). They have experience with ideation techniques and design iteration. They have not yet critically evaluated designs against design criteria and user stories, or used generative AI outputs as ideation input.
descriptors.endpoint: Students generate multiple design ideas using a range of ideation techniques, modify and evaluate them critically against design criteria and user stories, and communicate the preferred design with justification.

nodes.label: Generating multiple design ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use ideation techniques to generate multiple design ideas without prematurely evaluating them.
criteria: Produces at least two design ideas that are genuinely different approaches, not variations of the same idea
Uses an identifiable ideation technique

width.minimum: Generate at least two distinct design ideas for a problem using at least one ideation technique; ideas should be different from each other, not variations on the same approach.
width.typical: Use at least two different ideation techniques (e.g. mind mapping, role-play, graphic organiser, generative AI prompting) to generate a range of ideas; produce ideas that vary in approach rather than in surface features.
wider: Use generative AI model outputs as inspiration (not a direct solution) — explain how AI-generated outputs were used as a starting point and what human creative decisions were made from there
Investigate how design thinking frameworks structure the ideation phase — compare structured ideation with unstructured brainstorming and reflect on what each produces

nodes.label: Critically evaluating designs against criteria and user stories
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate design ideas critically by comparing them against design criteria and user stories to identify which ideas meet requirements and which do not.
criteria: Evaluation references specific design criteria, not just general preferences
Identifies at least one design that meets criteria better than alternatives and explains why
nodes.hinge_reason: N3 modification requires knowing which criteria are not met — students who evaluate by preference rather than criteria produce modifications without design rationale and cannot justify decisions at N4.

width.minimum: Evaluate at least two design ideas against at least two design criteria; explain which criteria each idea meets and which it fails.
width.typical: Evaluate a set of design ideas systematically against all design criteria and user stories; identify the strengths and weaknesses of each; explain trade-offs where an idea meets some criteria but not others.
wider: Use a formal design evaluation matrix (criteria vs ideas scoring) to compare designs, and reflect on whether the matrix captures all relevant considerations or oversimplifies
Evaluate designs against criteria that were not initially obvious — identify what the stakeholder would value that wasn't in the original criteria set

modes.reason: Students often evaluate designs by preference rather than against criteria. A structured reasoning approach — for each criterion: does this design meet it? how well? — builds the habit of evidence-based evaluation. Without structure, evaluation becomes rationalisation of a preferred design.

nodes.label: Modifying and developing the preferred design
nodes.checkpoint: Students can modify a design based on evaluation findings, in consultation with stakeholders, and further develop the preferred design toward implementation.
criteria: At least one modification is made and connected to a specific evaluation finding
The preferred design is developed with sufficient detail to guide the next phase

width.minimum: Make at least one modification to a design based on evaluation feedback; explain what criterion or user story the modification addresses.
width.typical: Review designs with stakeholders; make modifications to eliminate weaknesses identified in evaluation; develop the preferred design to a level of detail sufficient to guide implementation; document the design decisions made.
wider: Conduct a design review with the stakeholder and use their feedback to make modifications — document what was changed, what was retained, and why
Iterate through at least two design-evaluate-modify cycles and reflect on how the design improved with each iteration

nodes.label: Communicating the design
nodes.checkpoint: Students can communicate the preferred design and its rationale clearly to stakeholders.
criteria: Design is communicated with at least one visual representation
Rationale for choosing this design over alternatives is explained with reference to criteria or user stories

width.minimum: Present the preferred design with at least one visual representation and a brief explanation of why it was selected over alternatives.
width.typical: Communicate the preferred design using appropriate representations (mockups, diagrams, written specifications); explain the rationale for selecting this design over alternatives; address how it meets the key design criteria and user stories.
wider: Produce a design specification document that a different person could implement from without further clarification
Present the design to the stakeholder and handle questions and objections — revise the design or the communication in response to feedback

descriptors.title: Implement modular programs with OOP
descriptors.description: implement, modify and debug modular programs, applying selected algorithms and data structures, including in an object-oriented programming language
descriptors.knowledge: Students can implement, modify and debug programs involving control structures and functions (AC9TDI8P09). They have experience with iteration, selection, and basic functions. They have not yet implemented programs across multiple files or classes, applied data structures beyond simple lists, or written object-oriented code with custom classes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students implement, modify and debug modular programs using selected algorithms and data structures, including defining and using custom classes in an object-oriented programming language.

nodes.label: Applying data structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and use appropriate data structures (arrays, dictionaries, objects) to model structured data in their programs.
criteria: Program uses a data structure with more than one element
Student can explain why that data structure suits the data being stored
nodes.hinge_reason: Data structure selection errors propagate through all subsequent nodes — a student who uses a list where a dictionary is needed produces a program at N5 that is structurally incorrect and cannot be cleanly extended or debugged.

width.minimum: Use at least one data structure beyond a simple variable (e.g. list/array or dictionary) to store and access structured data in a program.
width.typical: Select appropriate data structures for different data needs — arrays for ordered sequential data, dictionaries/records for key-value data, objects for structured entities; justify the selection; access and manipulate stored data using the appropriate operations.
wider: Apply the binary search algorithm from a library to search sorted data — explain why binary search is faster than linear search and what preconditions it requires
Use multiple data structures in the same program and explain what each is responsible for modelling
Investigate how choosing the wrong data structure (e.g. using a list when a dictionary is needed) affects program complexity and performance

modes.reason: Data structure selection requires students to reason about the shape of the data and how it will be accessed. Students default to lists for everything. Multiple varied scenarios — ordered lists, character stats in RPGs, temperature records — each foreground a different data structure choice.

nodes.label: Defining custom classes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can define a custom class with attributes and methods that models an entity in their program.
criteria: Class definition includes at least two attributes and one method with correct syntax
At least one instance is created and the method is successfully called
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot define a class correctly cannot read or modify class-based code at N3, and cannot implement a modular OOP program at N5 — class syntax fluency is directly prerequisite.

width.minimum: Define a class with at least two attributes and one method; create at least one instance of the class and call the method.
width.typical: Define a class that models a real entity (e.g. book, character, sensor reading) with appropriate attributes and methods; create multiple instances; use the class to represent structured data in a program.
wider: Define a class with methods that track and modify the object's state over time — e.g. a library book class with methods to check out, return and reserve
Design and implement a class hierarchy with at least one subclass — explain what inheritance achieves and when it is and isn't appropriate
Refactor an existing program that uses dictionaries or parallel lists to use a custom class — explain what the refactor improves

modes.reason: OOP syntax and concepts require substantial practice. Students commonly confuse class definitions with instances, mix up self and instance variables, or misplace method definitions. Fluency with basic class definition and instantiation is a prerequisite for modular program design.

nodes.label: Reading and modifying modular programs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and interpret programs split across multiple functions, files or classes, and modify them to add functionality.
criteria: Correctly identifies what at least two modules/functions/classes do in a provided codebase
Makes a modification that works correctly without breaking existing functionality

width.minimum: Read a provided modular program (split across files or functions); identify what each module does; make one modification that adds or changes functionality.
width.typical: Read a program split across files, functions and/or classes; trace execution flow across modules; make modifications that add new functionality without breaking existing behaviour; explain how the modular structure made the modification easier.
wider: Extend a provided game codebase (e.g. an adventure game) by adding new characters, levels or abilities — identify where in the existing structure each addition belongs
Investigate how large codebases manage module dependencies and explain what problems arise when modules are tightly coupled

nodes.label: Debugging programs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate a bug in a program by reading error messages, printing variable state, and tracing execution; modify the program to fix the bug and verify the fix.
criteria: Identifies the location of the bug (not just the symptom)
Explains the cause of the bug before applying the fix
Verifies the fix produces correct output
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who guess at bug fixes without diagnosis cannot complete N5 — a modular program will always have bugs, and students who cannot systematically locate and explain bugs before fixing them produce programs with unfixed or newly introduced errors.

width.minimum: Given a program with a bug, identify the location of the error by reading the error message or printing variable values; explain what caused it; fix it and test the fix.
width.typical: Debug a program with at least two bugs using a systematic approach — read error messages, print or inspect variable state, trace execution, locate the cause, apply fix, test; document the debugging process.
wider: Debug a program where the error is a logic error (produces wrong output without crashing) rather than a syntax or runtime error — explain why logic errors are harder to find
Investigate and fix a bug in a larger modular program where the cause and symptom are in different modules

modes.reason: Debugging is systematic reasoning under uncertainty — students who guess at fixes without understanding the cause often make things worse. A structured approach (read error → form hypothesis about cause → test hypothesis by printing state → apply fix → verify) is the key skill and must be explicitly scaffolded.

nodes.label: Implementing a complete modular program
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write and edit a modular program that receives structured input, applies algorithms and data structures, and produces correct output.
criteria: Program is split into at least two logical modules (functions or classes)
Program produces correct output for at least two different test inputs
Program handles at least one edge case without crashing

width.minimum: Write a program that uses at least one custom class or function and processes structured input to produce output; the program produces correct output for a test input.
width.typical: Implement a program that is split into logical modules (functions and/or classes); the program processes structured input, applies appropriate data structures and algorithms, and produces correct output for the problem; test with multiple inputs.
wider: Write a program that reads structured data from a file (e.g. timestamped sensor data) and processes it to produce an output — such as a graph of an altitude sensor's flight path
Build a program that models a real inventory, library or tracking system using custom classes — implement the required methods to track state changes over time
Use a data structure from a library (e.g. binary search function) in a program and explain why using the library is preferable to reimplementing from scratch

modes.reason: Nodes 1–4 cover data structures, classes, reading modular code, and debugging separately. Implementation requires all of these simultaneously — choosing data structures, defining classes, organising modules, and debugging when things go wrong. Students who can do each individually often struggle when they must design the whole program architecture.

descriptors.title: Evaluate solutions against criteria and future impact
descriptors.description: evaluate existing and student solutions against the design criteria, user stories, possible future impact and opportunities for enterprise
descriptors.knowledge: Students can evaluate existing and student solutions against the design criteria, user stories and sustainability (AC9TDI8P10). They have experience applying criteria-based evaluation. They have not yet evaluated for future impact, unintended consequences of AI systems, or enterprise/pivot opportunities.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate existing and student solutions against design criteria, user stories, possible future impact (including unintended consequences) and opportunities for enterprise.

nodes.label: Evaluating against design criteria and user stories
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate a digital solution by judging its quality against specific design criteria and user stories.
criteria: Each criterion is assessed with specific evidence (not just yes/no)
Evaluation distinguishes between fully met, partially met and not met criteria
nodes.hinge_reason: Evidence-based criteria evaluation at N1 is prerequisite for N2 — identifying unintended consequences requires the same structured analytical approach; students who evaluate by preference produce consequence analysis that is similarly ungrounded.

width.minimum: Evaluate a solution against at least two design criteria; state clearly whether each criterion is met and provide evidence.
width.typical: Evaluate a solution systematically against all design criteria and user stories; for each criterion, provide evidence of whether it is met; identify areas where the solution partially meets criteria and explain what would be needed to fully meet them.
wider: Evaluate an existing product (e.g. a safety by design implementation in a social media platform) against criteria derived from the Safety by Design Vision — identify where it meets and fails to meet each criterion
Evaluate a student solution with a peer using shared criteria — compare independent evaluations and resolve disagreements about whether criteria are met

modes.reason: Evaluation requires evidence-based reasoning against criteria, not subjective opinion. Students without structure often evaluate by feel. A scaffold — criterion → evidence for → evidence against → judgement — produces defensible evaluations.

nodes.label: Evaluating future impact and unintended consequences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate a digital solution's possible future impact, including unintended consequences, and explain how design choices affect downstream outcomes.
criteria: Identifies at least one unintended consequence of the solution
Connects the consequence to a specific design decision or data choice
Suggests at least one change that would mitigate the identified consequence

width.minimum: Identify at least one possible unintended consequence of a digital solution and explain how the design decision contributed to it.
width.typical: Evaluate a digital solution's future impact — including intended benefits, possible unintended consequences, and how the design could be changed to mitigate negative impacts; consider impacts on diverse user populations.
wider: Examine how AI image generation solutions trained on homogeneous data produce outputs that fail to represent diverse users — explain the training data decision that caused this and what would mitigate it
Analyse the complexities of training predictive models on low-probability events (e.g. autonomous vehicle edge cases) and evaluate how solution design should account for these
Evaluate a solution's data privacy implications over time — what data is collected, retained, and what could be done with it beyond the original purpose

modes.reason: Unintended consequences are abstract without real-world cases. AI bias, autonomous vehicle edge cases, and privacy creep each illuminate a different category of future impact — together they build a more complete framework for impact assessment than any single example.

nodes.label: Evaluating for enterprise and pivot opportunities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how existing products have met the needs of different user groups and identify opportunities for enterprise or solution adaptation.
criteria: Identifies a specific product adaptation and the user need it addressed
Explains what changed in the product to serve the new user group

width.minimum: Describe one example of a digital product that has adapted to meet the needs of a different user group; explain what changed and what user need it addressed.
width.typical: Evaluate how existing products have pivoted to meet the needs of different users (e.g. how social media applications have expanded the types of media and interactions); identify what made the pivot possible and what new user needs it addressed.
wider: Identify an unmet user need in an existing product category and propose how a solution could be adapted or extended to address it — evaluate the feasibility of the adaptation
Examine how platforms that began with one user group have expanded (positively or negatively) to serve others — evaluate the design changes that enabled this

descriptors.title: Create interactive content for diverse audiences
descriptors.description: select and use emerging digital tools and advanced features to create and communicate interactive content for a diverse audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students can select and use a range of digital tools efficiently and responsibly to create and communicate content (AC9TDI8P11, AC9TDI8P12). They have experience with standard digital tools. They have not yet used emerging technologies for dynamic content, incorporated interactive elements, or designed specifically for accessibility.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select and use emerging digital tools and advanced features to create interactive content that is accessible and appropriate for a diverse audience.

nodes.label: Locating content with advanced search
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate relevant content using Boolean operators or AI-assisted search features to refine results.
criteria: Demonstrates use of at least one advanced search technique (Boolean operator or AI search feature)
Can explain why the search terms were chosen and how results were refined

width.minimum: Use Boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT) or an advanced search feature to locate content relevant to a specific need; explain how the search terms were refined.
width.typical: Use multiple search strategies — Boolean operators, advanced filters, AI similarity search — to locate relevant and credible content; evaluate the results for relevance and source quality; explain the reasoning behind search term choices.
wider: Compare results from Boolean operator search with AI-assisted search for the same information need — analyse what each approach surfaces and misses
Investigate how image similarity search works and use it to find visually similar content for a specific creative or analytical purpose

nodes.label: Adding interactive elements
nodes.checkpoint: Students can incorporate interactive elements into content that allow users to control and explore the information.
criteria: At least one interactive element changes what is displayed based on user input
The interaction serves a communicative purpose (helps users explore or understand the content)

width.minimum: Add at least one interactive element to a piece of content that changes what is shown based on user input (e.g. a slider, click-through, or filter).
width.typical: Create content with multiple interactive elements — sliders for time-series control, toggles, clickable regions — that allow users to explore the content actively; explain how each interaction helps users engage with the information.
wider: Build interactive content that incorporates real data with user-controlled parameters — for example, a slider that lets users explore how changing one variable affects a data relationship
Combine interactive elements with visualisations so that user interaction changes what data is displayed
Incorporate accessibility features into interactive content (e.g. keyboard navigation, ARIA labels) so that users who cannot use a mouse can still interact

modes.reason: Interactive content creation requires coordinating content, interaction design and technical implementation. Students often focus on technical implementation at the expense of whether the interaction actually helps users engage with the content. Integration here is designing the interaction to serve the communication goal, not just being technically functional.

nodes.label: Designing for accessibility
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use built-in accessibility features to ensure content is usable by people with diverse abilities.
criteria: At least one accessibility feature is implemented correctly
Student can explain who benefits from the feature and how
nodes.hinge_reason: The descriptor requires content for a diverse audience — students who have not engaged with accessibility principles at N3 produce N4 content that excludes users with different abilities, failing the descriptor's core requirement.

width.minimum: Apply at least one accessibility feature to a piece of content (e.g. ALT text for images, appropriate colour contrast, captions); explain who it benefits and how.
width.typical: Apply multiple accessibility features appropriate to the content type — ALT text for images, captions for video/audio, colour contrast checks, heading structure for screen readers — explain how each serves users with different abilities.
wider: Audit an existing piece of content for accessibility issues using accessibility checking tools; explain each issue found and implement fixes
Design content that is accessible-first — explain how designing for accessibility from the start differs from retrofitting it
Investigate how accessibility requirements are encoded in web standards (e.g. WCAG) and apply specific criteria to evaluate and improve a piece of content

modes.reason: Students often conflate accessibility with one group (e.g. visually impaired only). Multiple accessibility contexts — screen readers, cognitive accessibility, motor accessibility, captioning for deaf users — broaden the concept and prevent a too-narrow design response.

nodes.label: Creating interactive content for a diverse audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can combine emerging digital tools, interactive elements and accessibility features to create and communicate interactive content for a diverse audience.
criteria: Content uses at least one feature that goes beyond standard static content creation
At least one interactive element is included that serves the audience
At least one accessibility feature is present

width.minimum: Create interactive content using at least one advanced tool feature; include at least one interactive element; ensure content is accessible for at least one non-default audience.
width.typical: Create a piece of interactive content that uses emerging tools (e.g. AR overlay, interactive animation combining generative AI and human-created content), interactive elements, and accessibility features; explain how the design choices serve the intended diverse audience.
wider: Use an AR overlay triggered by a QR code to add dynamic information to physical content — explain how this extends the communication beyond what static content allows
Combine outputs from multiple generative AI sources (images, sounds, text) to produce an interactive animation or complex narrative — document the curation decisions made
Develop content for a specific underserved audience (e.g. a community group, accessibility users) and evaluate with representative users

modes.reason: Creating accessible, interactive content for a diverse audience requires coordinating advanced tools, interaction design, and accessibility features simultaneously. Students who can do each individually often produce content that prioritises one dimension at the expense of others. Integration here is ensuring all three serve the communication goal together.

descriptors.title: Plan and manage agile projects
descriptors.description: use simple project management tools to plan and manage individual and collaborative agile projects, accounting for risks and responsibilities
descriptors.knowledge: Students have experience with collaborative digital tools and sequencing tasks (AC9TDI8P12). They can assign roles and track progress. They have not yet applied agile project management techniques, worked with version control in a collaborative coding context, or systematically accounted for project risks.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use project management tools to plan and manage individual and collaborative agile projects, establishing clear responsibilities, managing risks, and applying relevant legislation or guidelines.

nodes.label: Planning with agile decomposition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can decompose a project into tasks, schedule them, and assign responsibilities to team members.
criteria: Project is decomposed into distinct tasks with assignments and due dates
Plan is recorded in a project management tool and accessible to all team members
nodes.hinge_reason: A project without a decomposed task structure makes N2 version control contributions uncoordinated (no tasks to commit against) and N3 risk identification abstract (no specific tasks to identify risks for).

width.minimum: Decompose a project into at least four tasks; assign each task to a team member with a due date; record in a project management tool.
width.typical: Decompose a project into sequenced tasks with dependencies; assign roles and responsibilities to all team members; use scheduling and revision to produce a realistic plan; explain the reasoning behind the task sequence.
wider: Use project management tool features (e.g. AI-assisted summaries, risk forecasting) to identify potential delays or bottlenecks and explain how the plan was adjusted
Apply an agile sprint structure — plan a sprint, execute, review, adjust — and reflect on what the sprint review revealed about the original plan

modes.reason: Project decomposition requires reasoning from the project goal backward through phases to specific tasks with dependencies — students who create flat task lists without sequencing or ownership produce plans that cannot be executed or tracked.

nodes.label: Collaborative version control
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a collaborative version control tool to manage shared code development, tracking changes and coordinating contributions.
criteria: At least two commits are made with meaningful commit messages
Contribution history shows individual contributions are trackable
nodes.hinge_reason: Version control workflow fluency is prerequisite for collaborative project execution — students who cannot commit, push and pull correctly lose each other's work and cannot demonstrate the collaborative project management the descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Make at least two contributions to a shared repository; explain what each contribution changed and why version control is useful.
width.typical: Use a collaborative version control tool (e.g. GitHub) to plan, decompose and manage contributions with peers; commit changes with meaningful messages; explain how version control prevents conflicting changes and maintains a history of work.
wider: Deliberately create a merge conflict and resolve it — explain what caused the conflict and how the resolution was reached
Use branching to develop a new feature independently of the main codebase and merge it when complete — explain what branches enable in team development

modes.reason: Version control workflows require precise procedural knowledge — staging, committing, pushing, pulling, resolving conflicts. Students need sufficient practice with the workflow before they can use it fluently in a collaborative context. Errors in this workflow cause lost work and confusion.

nodes.label: Identifying and managing risks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify project risks, assess their likelihood and impact, and plan mitigations for significant risks.
criteria: At least two distinct risks are identified (not the same risk stated differently)
Each risk has an identified mitigation that is specific and actionable

width.minimum: Identify at least two project risks; describe the potential impact of each and one mitigation for each.
width.typical: Identify a range of project risks (technical, team, timeline, legal); assess likelihood and impact; plan mitigations for significant risks; review risks as the project progresses and update mitigations.
wider: Apply a formal risk register approach — categorise risks, rate likelihood and impact, and plan responses (avoid, mitigate, accept, transfer) for each
Retrospectively analyse a project that did not go to plan — identify which risks materialised, which mitigations worked, and what should have been done differently

nodes.label: Applying relevant legislation and guidelines
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify relevant legislation and guidelines that apply to their project and explain how the project addresses each requirement.
criteria: At least one specific piece of legislation or guideline is identified and correctly described
Project plan includes at least one concrete action that addresses the legislative requirement

width.minimum: Identify at least one piece of legislation or guideline relevant to the project (e.g. data protection, copyright, privacy) and explain what it requires.
width.typical: Identify all relevant legislation and guidelines for the project; explain what each requires; demonstrate in the project plan or implementation how each requirement is being addressed.
wider: Evaluate an existing project or student solution for legal compliance — identify gaps and explain what changes would achieve compliance

Investigate the responsibilities that arise when collaborating with First Nations Australian community groups on digital solutions — including cultural protocols, permissions, attributions and privacy requirements — and document how each would be addressed in a project plan

modes.reason: Different legislative and guideline contexts (privacy law, copyright, Indigenous data sovereignty) each require different compliance actions — exposure to multiple contexts builds the habit of checking what applies rather than assuming all projects face the same requirements.

descriptors.title: Cyber security threat models
descriptors.description: develop cyber security threat models, and explore a software, user or software supply chain vulnerability
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how multi-factor authentication protects accounts and manage basic security settings (AC9TDI8P13). They understand access control concepts from AC9TDI10K01. They have not yet modelled how data moves through a system, constructed a threat model, or explored how specific vulnerabilities can be exploited.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop cyber security threat models to identify where data is at risk in a system, and explore a specific software, user or software supply chain vulnerability.

nodes.label: Data flow diagrams for threat modelling
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a data flow diagram to trace how private information moves through a system and identify where it is most at risk.
criteria: Data flow diagram correctly shows at least two data flows between system components
At least one threat is identified at a specific point in the diagram with an explanation of why that point is at risk
nodes.hinge_reason: Data flow diagrams are the analytical foundation for N2 and N3 — students who cannot map how data moves through a system cannot identify where it is at risk (N2) or trace the steps of exploiting a vulnerability (N3).

width.minimum: Draw a data flow diagram for a simple system showing at least two data flows; identify one point where the data could be at risk.
width.typical: Map how data moves between user, application and server in a web-based system using a data flow diagram; identify points where data is transmitted, stored, or processed; for each point, identify what threat exists and why that point is a target.
wider: Map data flows in a more complex system with multiple actors (user, server, third-party APIs) and identify threats at each boundary
Compare the data flow diagram for the same system with and without a specific security control — explain how the control changes the threat profile

modes.reason: Threat modelling requires systematic thinking — for every data flow, what is the threat? Students who approach security intuitively spot obvious threats (password interception) but miss subtler ones (session token exposure, plaintext in logs). The data flow diagram provides the structure that makes systematic threat identification possible.

nodes.label: Understanding vulnerability types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the nature of software, user and software supply chain vulnerabilities and explain how each can be exploited.
criteria: Correctly describes at least one vulnerability type
Explains a realistic path by which the vulnerability could be exploited (not just that it exists)

width.minimum: Describe at least one type of vulnerability (software, user, or supply chain) and explain how it could be exploited.
width.typical: Describe each of the three vulnerability types — software vulnerabilities (flaws in code), user vulnerabilities (social engineering, weak credentials), and software supply chain vulnerabilities (compromised dependencies); explain a realistic exploitation path for each.
wider: Research a real-world cyber attack and classify the vulnerabilities exploited — explain the exploitation chain
Investigate how prompt injection attacks can change the intended behaviour of generative AI models — explain why this is a software supply chain concern in AI-integrated systems
Examine how dependency vulnerabilities in software supply chains have caused high-profile breaches — explain what the vulnerability was and how it propagated

modes.reason: Vulnerability categories are best understood through distinct real-world cases — a social engineering example, a software bug example, and a supply chain example each illuminate a different attack surface. Students who only see one category often conflate the others.

nodes.label: Exploring a specific vulnerability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can systematically explore a specific vulnerability in their own software by tracing the exploitation path and observing the impact.
criteria: Identifies a specific vulnerability and traces at least the first step of exploitation
Describes the impact — what an attacker would gain or access as a result

width.minimum: Identify one vulnerability in a system (own or provided); trace the steps involved in exploiting it; describe what an attacker could access or do.
width.typical: Systematically explore a vulnerability in own software — map the exploitation path (e.g. changing a login cookie value to that of another user); observe the impact; explain what the vulnerability allows an attacker to do and why the system is susceptible.
wider: Explore an authentication bypass vulnerability and explain what access control decision it subverts — what should the system have checked that it didn't?
Investigate the full impact of a successfully exploited vulnerability — not just initial access but what data or capabilities become exposed as a consequence

descriptors.title: Apply Australian Privacy Principles
descriptors.description: apply the Australian Privacy Principles to critique and manage the digital footprint that existing systems and student solutions collect
descriptors.knowledge: Students can investigate and manage the digital footprint that existing systems and student solutions collect (AC9TDI8P14). They can identify what data systems collect about them. They have not yet applied the Australian Privacy Principles as a formal framework to critique systems, or used cryptographic techniques to protect user data in student solutions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply the Australian Privacy Principles to critique existing systems and manage the digital footprint collected by student solutions, including using appropriate technical controls to protect user data.

nodes.label: Understanding the Australian Privacy Principles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the key Australian Privacy Principles relevant to digital systems and describe what each requires.
criteria: Correctly identifies at least two APPs and their requirements
Can distinguish between requirements for collection, use and disclosure
nodes.hinge_reason: APP knowledge is directly prerequisite for N2 and N3 — students who cannot identify relevant principles cannot critique systems against them or implement compliant technical controls.

width.minimum: Identify at least two Australian Privacy Principles and describe what each requires a system to do or refrain from doing.
width.typical: Identify the APPs most relevant to digital systems (including those governing collection, use, disclosure, quality, security and access); describe what each requires; explain what type of data each applies to.
wider: Compare the Australian Privacy Principles with the EU GDPR — identify the key differences and explain what each framework is trying to achieve
Investigate what the APPs require for data collected about minors and explain how student-facing systems must address these requirements

modes.reason: The APPs are a set of distinct principles each with different requirements. Students need to accumulate sufficient examples of each principle in action before they can apply them to critique systems at N2 — a single APP in a single context does not build the evaluative toolkit N2 requires.

nodes.label: Critiquing existing systems against the APPs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can critique the extent to which existing digital systems allow users to control their data in line with the Australian Privacy Principles.
criteria: References a specific APP requirement (not just 'privacy in general')
Identifies evidence from the system that it does or does not comply
Proposes at least one specific change that would improve compliance

width.minimum: Critique one feature of an existing system (e.g. social media account settings) against at least one APP; identify whether the system complies and explain why or why not.
width.typical: Critique an existing system (e.g. a social media platform, school app) against multiple APPs — identify which requirements are met, which are violated, and what changes would bring the system into compliance.
wider: Audit a student-facing platform used at school against the APPs — document findings and propose a set of requirements for school procurement of digital tools

Investigate how social media platforms' data practices have changed in response to privacy regulations — identify what changed and whether the changes genuinely improve user control or primarily achieve legal compliance

modes.reason: APP critique requires students to apply a specific legal framework to system behaviour — this is structured legal reasoning, not opinion. A scaffold (identify the APP → what does it require? → what does the system do? → does it comply? → what would compliance look like?) produces rigorous analysis.

nodes.label: Protecting user data in student solutions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply technical controls in their own solutions to protect user data in line with the Australian Privacy Principles, including using cryptographic techniques for passwords.
criteria: At least one privacy risk in the student solution is identified and addressed with a technical control
Student can explain what the control protects against and what it would not protect against

width.minimum: Identify one type of personally identifiable data in a student solution and implement at least one technical control to protect it (e.g. not publicly displaying it, or explaining why cryptographic hashing should be used for passwords).
width.typical: Evaluate the student solution against the APPs; implement appropriate technical controls for each identified privacy risk — including using cryptographic hashing for passwords, limiting data collection to what is necessary, and ensuring PII is not publicly accessible without consent.
wider: Implement password hashing using a cryptographic hash function in a student solution and explain why storing hashed passwords rather than plaintext prevents a data breach from exposing users to password reuse attacks
Design a data minimisation strategy for a student solution — identify what data is strictly necessary and remove or anonymise what is not
Investigate what technical and organisational controls an organisation must combine to fully meet the APP security requirements — explain why technical controls alone are insufficient

modes.reason: Applying APPs to a student solution requires integrating legal understanding (which APPs apply), design decisions (what data is collected and why), and technical implementation (how to protect it). Students who understand each independently often fail to connect them — the integration is applying the framework to their own work systematically rather than as an afterthought.
